title: Implementation: Making It All Happen
overview: Chapter 14 closes The Skilled Helper by turning from planning to action. Egan explains why clients fail to start or sustain change, distinguishes decisional from protracted self-control, and follows Mara as she acts on her goals amid a family financial crisis. He sets out five principles of effective implementation (overcoming procrastination, avoiding imprudent action, identifying obstacles and resources through force-field analysis, finding incentives and rewards, and using action-focused self-contracts), then discusses social support, challenging relationships, two-way feedback and checklists. The shadow side of implementation covers passive helpers, client inertia and entropy. A long section on resilience covers outcome and process resilience, contributing factors and posttraumatic growth. Egan then addresses ending helping - getting along without a helper, illustrated by Vicky's self-managed bipolar disorder - and clients who choose not to change, before revisiting the key ingredients of successful therapy.
objectives: Explain the difference between planning and action using the Action Arrow, and describe decisional and protracted self-control.
Describe the five principles of effective implementation, including strategy, tactics and logistics.
Apply force-field analysis to identify obstacles and facilitating resources.
Explain the role of incentives, extinction and self-contracts in sustaining action.
Discuss social support, challenging relationships and two-way (confirmatory and corrective) feedback.
Analyse the shadow side of implementation: reluctant helpers, client inertia and entropy.
Define resilience, distinguish outcome and process resilience, list contributing factors and explain posttraumatic growth.
Describe Egan's view of ending helping, including getting along without a helper and choosing not to change.
List the key ingredients of successful therapy as revisited by Egan.

sections.heading: Introduction to Implementation
sections.detailed:
Planning versus action. Figure 14.1 shows the Action Arrow of the helping model. Egan points out that Stages I, II and III, with their nine tasks, are all about planning for change rather than change itself. Throughout the book, however, he has insisted that action must be built into planning and planning into action: the "little actions" that get change moving start right from the beginning. The Action Arrow says that problem-managing action should start immediately, continue throughout the helping process and lead to the client's preferred outcomes. Chapter 14 takes a more formal look at results-producing action, at the obstacles that block it, and at ways of getting past them.

Morris's conditions for success. In True Success, Tom Morris (1994) lists the conditions for achieving success, and Egan notes that all of them belong to the problem-management process: knowing what you want (a goal that is powerfully imagined); focus and concentration in preparing and planning; confidence in yourself to see the goal through, that is, self-efficacy; committing emotional energy; consistency and persistence in pursuing the goal; integrity that inspires trust and gets others pulling for you; and the capacity to enjoy the journey. The first two relate to Stages II and III, while the other five are about implementing what has been imagined and planned. The counsellor's role is to help clients engage in these internal and external behaviours for the sake of goal accomplishment.

Clients differ in how readily they act. Some clients, once they know what to do, simply go ahead, with or without a formal plan; they find resources within themselves or get support and challenge from significant others, and need little more from the helper. Others choose goals and devise strategies but get stuck when it comes to action. Most clients fall somewhere between these extremes.

Why people fail to start or give up. Discipline and self-control, which are aspects of self-responsibility, matter a great deal in implementation. Kirschenbaum (1987) found many contributors to not starting or to giving up: low initial commitment, weak self-efficacy, poor outcome expectations, self-punishment instead of self-reward, depressive thinking, failure to cope with emotional stress, inconsistent self-monitoring, not using effective habit-change techniques, yielding to social pressure, failing to cope with an early relapse, and attending to the wrong things, such as the difficulty of change rather than the attractiveness of the outcome. Egan observes that this is the opposite of what Morris recommends.

Decisional and protracted self-control. Kanfer and Schefft (1988) distinguished two kinds of self-control. In decisional self-control, one choice ends a conflict, as when a woman decides to leave an abusive spouse and carries it out. In protracted self-control, continued resistance to temptation is needed, as with a client with serious health problems who must stay committed to a demanding diet, exercise and stress-reduction programme day after day, renewing her resolve every time she is tempted. It helps if she treats temptations as learning opportunities rather than battles, and finds ways to make the struggle tolerable or even rewarding; one client munched a carrot whenever tempted and joked to himself about it. Most clients need both kinds. Someone who decides to give up alcohol completely (decisional) must also manage the inevitable long-term temptations (protracted). Protracted self-control calls for a preventive mentality and some street smarts: it is easier to decline an invitation to a bar than to sit in one all evening and not drink.
sections.simple: Stages I to III are about planning; implementation is about actually doing it. Egan says action should start right away and continue throughout helping. People give up for many reasons, so they need both a one-time decision (decisional self-control) and ongoing resistance to temptation (protracted self-control).
keyPoints: The Action Arrow: action should start immediately, continue throughout helping and lead to preferred outcomes.
Morris's seven conditions of success: the first two fit Stages II and III, the other five fit implementation.
Kirschenbaum (1987) listed many reasons people fail to start or give up, e.g. low commitment, weak self-efficacy, self-punishment.
Kanfer and Schefft: decisional self-control (one choice ends a conflict) vs protracted self-control (continued resistance to temptation).
Most clients need both kinds; protracted self-control needs a preventive mentality and street smarts.

sections.heading: Mara Moves into Action
sections.detailed:
Small actions and a bias toward action. Egan reviews the plans Mara has made, alone and with Carlos, and follows how she carries them out through the chapter. He notes the section title is a little unfair, since Mara has been taking many "small actions" all along, showing the bias toward action described in Chapter 2. Her case shows that designing and implementing change is not precision engineering; people and their problems are too messy. She can be blown off course, as her disastrous conversation with her father nearly did, but she is resilient and her aspirations empower her.

Goal one: community. A top priority is her social life. In Iran she found ready-made communities; now she must build her own. When Carlos asks whether a close relationship with a man is part of this, she says she wants to play that by ear and prefers it to develop within a larger community, noting that her relationship with Jim was too private. Egan adds that if building community meant deciding to leave her parents' home (decisional self-control), she would need to understand how much protracted self-control would be required to handle separation, guilt and early loneliness.

Stepping back with two-way feedback. The feedback routine at the start and end of every session has helped Mara a great deal. Carlos suggests they look at the bigger picture, and Mara asks for ten minutes to prepare. The review shows she feels on the right track. Building a community of friends and colleagues is still the top goal; there is no Iranian-American community nearby, but Iranian cultural values can still shape her choice of friends and activities. She recognises that her ideal community may be partly an idealisation of her trip.

Goal two: career. Her career goal has shifted from a bigger managerial role in her father's business to preparing herself for a more fulfilling career in the business world. She is considering an MBA and has contacted a group called "Women in Business," for which her quasi-managerial role makes her a good fit.

Parents and moods. She is unsure whether "normalising" her relationship with her parents is a real goal, because they do not co-own it and her father's "case-closed" attitude blocks cooperation; her mother remains a shadow figure. Emotionally she has been "all over the place": exhilarated when moving toward her goals, flat at the dealership, where work has lost its meaning because the business has stalled and may even have to be sold at a low price given her father's health. The dead-end feel depresses her, and she has to work hard to dig herself out. Egan uses this mixture of hope, sadness and challenge to introduce the work clients must do to act on their goals.
sections.simple: Mara has been taking small actions all along. A review with Carlos shows her goals: build a community of friends, prepare for a more fulfilling business career, and an uncertain goal of normalising things with her parents. Her moods swing between exhilaration and flatness.
keyPoints: Mara shows a bias toward action through many small steps; change is not precision engineering.
Top goal: building a community of friends and colleagues, not just a one-to-one relationship.
Leaving home would be decisional self-control but would demand protracted self-control too.
Career goal shifted to preparing for a more fulfilling business career (MBA, 'Women in Business').
Normalising the relationship with her parents is unclear as a goal because they do not co-own it.

sections.heading: Help Clients Move from Planning to Action: Principles of Effective Implementation
sections.detailed:
The readiness dilemma. Norcross, Krebs and Prochaska (2011) warn helpers not to treat all clients as if they were in the action stage, because most arrive not ready to act. This is a dilemma, since the sooner clients act on their own behalf, the more likely they are to succeed. The helper's job is to bridge that gap. Johancen-Walt (2010) adds that therapy progress is often an accumulation of small changes, plateaus and regressions, so both client and helper need patience.

Strategy, tactics and logistics. In implementation, strategies have to be complemented by tactics and logistics. A strategy is a practical plan or programme for achieving an objective. Tactics is the art of adapting a plan to the immediate situation, including changing it on the spot to deal with unforeseen complications. Logistics is the art of providing the resources a plan needs, in a timely way.

The case of Rebecca. Rebecca wanted to take a summer evening statistics course so that her next first semester would be lighter, leaving time to act in a school play. Her university required prepayment, and she would not have her summer earnings in time. She quickly found the same course at a nearby community college where, as a local resident, her tuition was minimal. She kept her overall plan (strategy), adapted it to an unforeseen circumstance (tactics) and found another resource (logistics).

Why principles are needed. Because many well-meaning, motivated clients are poor tacticians and poor at finding resources, counsellors add value by applying a set of principles that help clients engage in focused and sustained goal-accomplishing action. The chapter sets out five: help clients overcome procrastination; help them avoid imprudent action; help them identify possible obstacles to and resources for implementing plans; help them find incentives and rewards for sustained action; and help them develop action-focused self-contracts. Box 14.2 later adds related guidelines such as forming implementation intentions, developing contingency plans and acquiring needed skills.
sections.simple: Most clients are not ready to act when they arrive, yet early action predicts success. Plans need strategy (the plan), tactics (adapting it on the spot) and logistics (getting resources in time). Egan then gives five principles for helping clients act.
keyPoints: Norcross, Krebs and Prochaska: do not treat all clients as if they are in action.
Johancen-Walt: progress is small changes, plateaus and regressions, so patience is needed.
Strategy = practical plan; tactics = adapting it to the situation; logistics = timely resources.
Rebecca's statistics course illustrates all three.
Five principles: overcome procrastination, avoid imprudent action, identify obstacles and resources, find incentives, use self-contracts.

sections.heading: Help Clients Overcome Procrastination
sections.detailed:
The knowing-doing gap and hidden commitments. Some clients keep putting action off. The "knowing-doing gap" (Kegan & Lahey, 2010; Pfeffer & Sutton, 2000) has always been with us. Egan recalls the "competing agendas" of Chapter 12; Kegan and Lahey go further and describe "hidden commitments" that block change. A school principal believes she should spend more time in classrooms but never finds the time. She may fear disrupting a comfortable faculty culture, or fear being embarrassed in maths and science classes; the hidden commitment behind that is that authority figures should stay on a pedestal to keep order. Everyone has such commitments, and helpers should challenge their own and help clients see and challenge theirs.

Immunity to change and short-term pain. There are many other reasons for procrastination (Ferrari, 2010; Ferrari, Johnson & McCowan, 1995; Pychyl, 2010). Each person's set of factors creates what Kegan and Lahey call a personal "immunity to change." Many clients procrastinate because they focus on the short-term pain of acting even when they see the long-term benefits.

Eula and second-order procrastination. Eula wanted to start a software firm for the family-business market, but a year passed without a product. She was busy with useful activities such as research, seminars, contacts with professionals, business plans and a brochure, but none produced products. Her counsellor helped her see that she was afraid of starting the business, and that overpreparation and many half-finished products were signs of that fear. She finished one product and marketed it online; it was modestly successful, "the cork was out of the bottle," and further products followed. Eula was not lazy, but she fell into what Andreou (2007) calls second-order procrastination: putting off implementing a solution to procrastination itself, avoiding the most critical actions.

Mara and assertiveness. Mara procrastinates only when she needs to be assertive. Volunteering with her college alumni group, she was given solitary clerical work. Carlos wondered aloud whether it could become a win for both sides. She had not told her contact what she wanted because she did not want to seem selfish, which opened a fruitful discussion about how her "selflessness" pervades her life, especially with her parents, and why it is not the antidote to the selfishness she dislikes. She then met the alumni director and easily found work with others.

True and false urgency. The opposite of procrastination is a sense of urgency that leads to timely action. Kotter (2008) argues that change does not start, continue or stick without urgency, but distinguishes true urgency (doing the right things in a timely way) from false urgency (lots of frenzied activity that goes nowhere). Egan asks whether Mara, who is always busy except when depressed, is busy about the right things.

Good procrastination. Finally, Partnoy (2012) suggests procrastination is not all bad: delay gives clients time to think about consequences, especially of acting too fast. There is good and bad procrastination.
sections.simple: Procrastination often comes from hidden commitments that make people immune to change, or from focusing on short-term pain. Eula kept busy but avoided the key step of finishing products. Real urgency means doing the right things on time, not just being busy, and some delay can even be useful.
keyPoints: Knowing-doing gap (Kegan & Lahey; Pfeffer & Sutton); hidden commitments create 'immunity to change'.
Many procrastinate by focusing on the short-term pain of acting.
Eula: second-order procrastination (Andreou) - delaying the solution to procrastination itself.
Kotter: true urgency (right things, timely) vs false urgency (frenzied activity going nowhere).
Partnoy: there is good and bad procrastination.

sections.heading: Help Clients Avoid Imprudent Action
sections.detailed:
Acting too fast. For some clients the problem is not refusal to act but acting imprudently, such as rushing into the first "strategy" that comes to mind.

The case of Elmer. After two back operations, Elmer was told further surgery would not help, and he faced chronic pain that worsened when he was anxious or depressed. While working with a counsellor, he read about a pain clinic in a western state and, without consulting anyone, signed up for a six-week programme. Within ten days he was back, more depressed than ever. The holistic programme, which covered nutrition, stress management, problem solving, interpersonal life and group training in behavioural pain management, aimed at reducing and managing pain rather than eliminating it. Elmer had bought a "packaged" programme without studying it, expecting medical marvels.

Two mistakes. Elmer's goal of being completely pain-free was never tested for realism; a realistic goal would have been reducing and managing pain. His counsellor failed to help him avoid two errors: setting an unrealistic goal and, in desperation, acting on the first strategy that appeared. Action cannot be prudent when it rests on flawed assumptions.

Mara rethinks a plan. After her father's outburst and his dismissal of a second approach ("That issue has been settled"), Mara slowly regained confidence. She "more or less" decided to tell her mother her plans, knowing her mother would tell her father. Carlos asked her to explore the "more or less." It turned out to mean avoiding telling her father directly, doubt about whether this was the most moral way to act, and not having explored the possible fallout. She concluded she must rethink how to be both honest and prudent with her parents.
sections.simple: Some clients act too quickly, grabbing the first strategy they see. Elmer joined a pain clinic expecting to be pain-free and came back more depressed. Prudent action needs realistic goals and careful choice of strategy.
keyPoints: Imprudent action = rushing into the first strategy that comes to mind.
Elmer chose a pain clinic without checking it and with an unrealistic pain-free goal.
His counsellor missed two errors: an unrealistic goal and acting on the first strategy.
Action based on flawed assumptions cannot be prudent.
Carlos helps Mara explore her 'more or less' decision so she can be honest and prudent.

sections.heading: Help Clients Identify Possible Obstacles to and Resources for Implementing Plans
sections.detailed:
Force-field analysis. Kurt Lewin (1969) codified common sense in "force-field analysis": a client's review of the major obstacles to, and major facilitating forces for, carrying out action plans. The slogan is "forewarned is forearmed."

Obstacles (restraining forces). Identifying likely obstacles forewarns clients. Raul and Maria, a childless couple, planned with a counsellor to adopt: examining motivation, reviewing suitability, contacting an agency and preparing for an interview. They then identified two pitfalls: negative feelings when scrutinised by an adoption agency, and helplessness and frustration from the long, uncertain process. The assumption is that clients who know the "wrinkles" will be less disoriented when they meet them. Done well, this is a straightforward census of likely pitfalls, not a self-defeating search for everything that could go wrong. Obstacles can arise from within clients, from other people, from their social settings and from larger environmental forces. Sometimes awareness alone helps clients mobilise resources; sometimes an explicit coping strategy is needed. The counsellor role-played a tough adoption examiner in two sessions, which helped the couple stay calm in real interviews, and linked them with a mutual-help group of adopting parents.

Facilitating forces (resources). Counsellors can also help clients find unused resources. Nora found weekly dialysis depressing and wondered whether life tied to a machine was worth living. Her counsellor showed her that her discouraging thoughts made things harder and helped her broaden her thinking. A religious person, she began reading the Bible the day before treatment and meditating on it during travel and treatment, replacing "poor-me" thinking with positive thinking, an underused resource. Brainstorming facilitating forces raises the probability that clients act in their interests, and resources can be simple: George, avoiding an invasive diagnostic test, asked a friend to accompany him, which committed him to go and distracted him from his fears.

Obstacles can appear any time: Mara's "Obstacle with a capital O." Mara was progressing socially and in career preparation, enjoying her Women at Work group, where she both received help and used her managerial experience to help others. Then her father announced that the car company was closing the dealership within two months and that he had lost almost two-thirds of his pension money through a risky broker. The dealership was to have provided for Mara and her mother; the settlement would be modest. Their financial world was collapsing.

Mara's response. She called an emergency session, but Carlos found her unexpectedly composed and ready to work. She saw good and bad news: no job in two months, but the way to a new career was open; a recession loomed, but she trusted her ability to find fitting work; building friends and associates, now called networking, mattered more than ever. Egan notes she had taken to heart an overall goal of helping: learning to apply problem management on her own, and seeing the opportunities hidden in problems. The crisis also confronted her with what she had avoided: fear for her father and mother. She now had three broad goals - a new social life, a new career path and a new relationship with her parents - each involving second-order change. Together they were massive second-order change, but they fed into one another and made each other easier. Some problems cannot be solved or managed but must be transcended. She did not yet know what resetting her relationship with her parents would look like, but was confident, and Carlos was her consultant.
sections.simple: Force-field analysis means listing what will block a plan and what will help it. Knowing the likely obstacles ahead of time, and rehearsing how to cope, reduces shock, while finding unused resources makes action more likely. Mara's family crisis became an obstacle she turned into an opportunity.
keyPoints: Lewin's force-field analysis: review restraining (obstacles) and facilitating forces; 'forewarned is forearmed'.
Obstacles come from within, from others, from social settings and from wider environmental forces.
Raul and Maria: role-play and a mutual-help group helped them cope with adoption obstacles.
Nora (Bible reading) and George (taking a friend) show simple facilitating resources.
Mara's family financial crisis led to three intersecting goals involving second-order change.

sections.heading: Help Clients Find Incentives and Rewards for Sustained Action
sections.detailed:
The basic principle. Clients avoid action programmes when the incentives and rewards for not acting outweigh those for acting.

Miguel: a tough approach. Miguel, a police officer tried for excessive force against a young offender, saw a counsellor through his HMO. His brutality had a long history: a bully on the beat, a despot at home, in run-ins at bars. His badge had become a licence. Arrest and trial shocked him from feeling invulnerable to feeling vulnerable. Found guilty, he was suspended and put on probation on condition that he continue counselling. Fear of consequences was a strong incentive and he had changed a great deal. The counsellor confronted him for remaining an adolescent, hiding behind his badge and using "cheap power," and told him fear would fade after probation and was a weak man's crutch. More positively, he saw a decent person beneath the tough exterior and argued that the real incentives lay there. He had Miguel picture a "tough but decent" cop, family man and friend, and devise "experiments in decency" at home, on the beat and with friends to experience the rewards of decency. He did not try to change Miguel's personality, which he did not believe possible, but pushed him to bring out a more constructive set of incentives that would drive out the old. Egan asks readers whether this approach fits responsible helping and what they would do.

Incentives that start change may not sustain it: Dwight. Partially paralysed after a work accident, Dwight began rehabilitation with commitment but months later wanted to quit. His counsellor asked him to visit the children's ward, where he was struck by a teenager on chemotherapy. They supported each other; when the boy died three months later, Dwight felt he could not give up without letting him down. The counsellor celebrated this incentive but also helped Dwight find "backup" incentives for when current ones lose power.

Extinction: Luigi. Constructive activities that are not rewarded tend to lose vigour, decrease and disappear; this is extinction. Luigi had stayed out of mental hospitals for three years by working at a soup kitchen, but was becoming manic. Counselling revealed he now worked there from "should" rather than "want," feeling guilty about leaving and fearing relapse; the work no longer interested or challenged him. He moved to a group housing the homeless and elderly, poured energy into it, and his manic episodes subsided. The lesson: incentives cannot be set up and taken for granted; they need tending.
sections.simple: People act when the rewards for acting outweigh the rewards for not acting. Miguel's counsellor helped him find incentives in being decent rather than in fear. Incentives that start change may fade, so backups are needed, and unrewarded actions die out (extinction).
keyPoints: Clients avoid action when rewards for not acting outweigh rewards for acting.
Miguel: a confrontational counsellor replaced fear with incentives from 'decency' via experiments in decency.
Dwight: incentives that start change may not keep it going; build backup incentives.
Extinction: unrewarded constructive activity fades and disappears (Luigi).
Incentives need tending; they cannot be taken for granted.

sections.heading: Help Clients Develop Action-Focused Self-Contracts
sections.detailed:
Contracts focus energy. Self-contracts, discussed earlier as a way of committing to goals, also help clients start and sustain problem-managing and opportunity-developing action. Self-contracts and agreements with others focus clients' energies.

Social support has to be enrolled. Sherman and associates (2008) describe obstacles to getting family, spouses, partners and friends to support veterans with PTSD. Family members hold back because nobody asked them, they live far away, they hold unchallenged beliefs (such as not discussing what happens behind closed doors), they are reluctant to try to understand the veteran, and they fear upsetting information. Spouses and partners distrust formal programmes, feel hopeless about improvement, resign themselves to lifelong caregiving and feel their attention belongs with their children. Perhaps the main problem is that support does not happen automatically; client, helper and others must make it happen, and relevant parties must be enrolled.

Commitment contracts. Karlan (2008) shows the power of commitment contracts. His website, stickK, lets people set a goal, decide the stakes for not pursuing it, choose a referee to judge progress and get supporters' help. Public commitment works: sharing a change agenda with others makes it easier to move forward and harder to quit. Karlan's principles - goal setting, putting stakes at risk, an objective referee and transparency - can be adapted for therapy.

The seventh-grader. A boy disrupted class with verbal jousting and profanity to build a reputation among friends for fearlessness; punishments were dwarfed by peer admiration. The school counsellor convened the boy, parents, teacher and principal and proposed a simple contract: after a disruption he would spend the next day working alone under a teacher's aide, away from friends, then return with no further punishment. Meanwhile the counsellor worked with him on what classroom "leadership" might look like. He spent many days with the aide in month one, two days in month two and one in month three. He really wanted to be with classmates, so he paid the price of self-control. He also found constructive leadership, such as challenging the teacher's ideas and sparking lively debate that even the teacher valued. This was more than a self-contract: involving other stakeholders increases the likelihood of progress. The more helpers know about incentives, the more clients benefit.
sections.simple: Contracts, with oneself and with others, focus effort on action. Support from family does not happen by itself; people must be enrolled. Karlan's stickK shows that goals, stakes, a referee and going public all help, as the seventh-grader's contract showed.
keyPoints: Self-contracts help clients both start and sustain action.
Sherman and associates: many obstacles stop families supporting veterans with PTSD; support must be enrolled.
Karlan's stickK: goal, stakes, referee, supporters; public commitment works.
Principles adaptable to therapy: goal setting, stakes at risk, objective referee, transparency.
The seventh-grader's multi-stakeholder contract cut disruptions and fostered constructive leadership.

sections.heading: Social Support and the Importance of Challenge
sections.detailed:
Social support as a resource. Planning includes identifying internal and environmental resources, and social support is one of the most important (Barker & Pistrang; Seeman; Taylor). Surprisingly, research verifying its usefulness is thin (Cruza-Guet and associates; Hogan, Linden & Najarian; Roehrle & Strouse), so common sense must sometimes outpace science. Lakey (2010) argues the helping professions still lack enough understanding of support processes to build effective new interventions. The starting point is the client and the relationship with the support provider; the kind and quality of that relationship probably matters most. Supposedly supportive people or actions are supportive only if the client perceives them so, and how support is given is critical; well-meaning supporters are sometimes shunned.

What the evidence shows. Most practitioners still see support as key. The Basic Behavioral Science Task Force of the National Advisory Mental Health Council (1996) reported that in about 75% of studies with clinically depressed patients, social-support factors increased initial treatment success and helped maintain gains, and that in schizophrenia and alcoholism higher support went with fewer relapses, fewer hospitalisations and better maintenance of gains. Helpers can give much support, but if clients pursue goals in their real lives, their main support should be there too.

Declining social capital. Putnam (2000) shows that in North American society "social capital" - informal connectedness and formal civic engagement - has fallen: fewer organisations, less contact with neighbours, friends and even family. Yet this is where clients must change.

Social facilitation. Wing and Jeffery (1999) found that weight-loss clients who enlisted friends were much more successful at losing weight and keeping it off than those who went solo. This "social facilitation" differs from dependence: facilitation energises, dependence often limits and depresses.

Two kinds of clients. Some lead impoverished social lives; the aim is to help them find social resources and get back into community. Others have people to turn to but, as Putnam notes, do not use them well; the task is to help them tap those resources. Casey, a much-travelled bachelor with friends scattered worldwide and no primary caregiver, recovered slowly after illness for lack of support. His counsellor challenged him to ask local friends for help, which he had avoided so as not to be a "burden." They were willing, and he also hesitantly "grafted" caring people from a local church onto his network; rather than piety, he found socially intelligent people who knew how much care to give, mostly simple friendship.

Distress drives supporters away. The same Council report found that highly distressed people, who most need support, may be least likely to get it because their distress drives supporters off. Distressed clients can learn to modulate their expressions of distress, and supporters can learn to deal with distressed friends, even "whiners."

Mara. Carlos gives Mara an article on social support and culture (Kim, Sherman & Taylor, 2008). She feels she straddles collectivistic and individualistic cultures, often losing the advantages and bearing the disadvantages of both. A "Who am I?" conversation helps her see how alone she has been without feeling lonely; her isolation is not debilitating but not helping, and she needs more support for her demanding agendas.
sections.simple: Social support is one of the most important resources for change, though research on it is thin. Support only counts if the client sees it as support. Clients who enlist friends do better (social facilitation), but very distressed people can push supporters away, and modern society offers less social capital.
keyPoints: Social support is a key resource, but research verifying it is skimpy; the relationship with the supporter matters most (Lakey).
NAMHC Task Force (1996): support aided treatment success and maintenance in depression, schizophrenia and alcoholism.
Putnam: social capital has declined in North America.
Wing and Jeffery: social facilitation (enlisting friends) aided weight loss; it differs from dependence.
Two client groups: those with impoverished social lives and those who do not use the support they have (Casey).
Highly distressed people may drive supporters away; both sides can learn to manage this.

sections.heading: Challenging Relationships
sections.detailed:
Support plus challenge. Support without challenge can be hollow, and challenge without support can be abrasive. Ideally, people in clients' lives provide a judicious mix of encouragement and challenge.

The case of Harry. In his early fifties Harry had drastic emergency surgery and recovered quickly, but problems with post-operative drugs made him ill and he adopted the mannerisms of a chronic invalid, persisting even after the right drugs were found: shuffling instead of walking tall, constantly discussing symptoms and using his condition to excuse himself from normal activities. His friends at first gave every kind of support, then realised his style would alienate others and keep him out of life. Support alone was not enough. Using various means, some with dark humour, they invited him to challenge himself: mocking his invalid movements, holding serious one-to-one talks, ignoring his talk of symptoms and routinely including him in plans. Harry did not always respond graciously but admitted he was lucky to have such friends. He died three years later but lived a full life until the end. Counsellors can support clients in finding people who will provide this mix.

Mara and confidants. Mara admits her only challenging relationship is with Carlos; her relationship with her father is dysfunctional rather than positively challenging, and with her mother bland. Carlos makes two points. First, she is not alone: McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Brashears (2006) confirm Putnam's thesis that Americans increasingly "bowl alone," with many having no one to confide in about their most important issues - the people who form one's core network of confidants. Second, her goal of building a community is designed to remedy this. Mara recalls that young people in Iran talked freely about aspirations, social strictures and the regime, but not about personal problems, relationships or religion; still, they were not "bowling alone." She now sees the kind of community she wants and says she needs confidants outside counselling.
sections.simple: Good relationships mix support with challenge. Harry's friends lovingly challenged his invalid behaviour, and he lived fully. Many people have no confidants, and Mara realises she needs some outside counselling.
keyPoints: Support without challenge is hollow; challenge without support is abrasive.
Harry's friends used support plus challenge (even dark humour) to keep him on the road to recovery.
Counsellors can help clients find people who give encouragement and challenge.
McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Brashears: many Americans have no one to confide in ('bowling alone').
Mara realises she wants confidants beyond her counsellor.

sections.heading: Two-Way Feedback
sections.detailed:
Feedback within sessions. Feedback was identified in Chapter 1 as a key ingredient of successful therapy (Lambert, 2010a). Feedback on progress toward outcomes at the start of each session, and on the quality and value of the session's interactions at the end, is a principal contributor to implementation; neither client nor helper can hide. If therapy is defined by life-enhancing outcomes, two-way feedback is crucial because it allows course correction. Dorner (1996) found that successful project managers reviewed progress, looked for unintended consequences and corrected course often, and the same applies to clients and helpers.

Feedback from everyday life. Feedback from significant others helps clients start acting and persevere when things get rough. Gilbert (1978) claimed improved information has more potential than anything else for building competence in managing performance. Feedback provides encouragement and challenge. Clients need adequate information on how they are doing; clear goals and paths let them judge progress, but sometimes a more objective view is needed. The purpose is not to judge but to give information, guidance, support and challenge.

Two kinds. Confirmatory feedback: significant others (helpers, relatives, friends, colleagues) tell clients they are on course. Corrective feedback: they tell clients they have wandered off course and specify what is needed to get back on.

Principles for corrective feedback. Help clients give feedback to themselves; give it in a spirit of caring; treat mistakes as opportunities for growth; mix confirmatory and corrective feedback; be concrete, specific, brief and to the point; focus on behaviour rather than elusive personality traits; help clients see whether behaviour helps or hinders goals; help them explore its impact and implications; avoid impatient negative language; give feedback in moderate doses, since overwhelming defeats the purpose; engage clients in dialogue, inviting them to comment and expand, because lectures rarely help; help clients discover alternatives, making suggestions if needed; and help them explore the upside of changing and the downside of not changing.

Confirmatory feedback should follow the same spirit. People often give detailed corrective feedback but only "nice job" for good work. A father praising his son Paul for standing up for a bullied friend described specifically what Paul did - stood his ground calmly and forcefully, did not apologise, accepted consequences - and its impact, even on the father himself. Specific behaviour plus impact turns praise into learning. A key problem is finding people who see the client in action often enough, care enough and have the skills to give feedback constructively.

Mara and Box 14.1. Mara has no one yet who could give such feedback; at work she gets only indirect signs she is doing well. She notes Carlos helps her give feedback to herself and wonders whether direct feedback from him would violate his method. Box 14.1 lists questions clients can ask themselves when implementing plans: how to move into action; what kind of self-starter they are and how to improve; what obstacles lie ahead and which are critical; how to manage them; how to keep efforts from flagging; what to do when they feel like giving up; what support will keep them going; what role hope plays; and what their track record is with life-enhancing change.
sections.simple: Feedback at the start (on progress) and end (on the session) of every meeting keeps therapy on course. Confirmatory feedback says you are on track; corrective feedback says you are off track and how to get back. Good feedback is caring, specific, behavioural, moderate and part of a dialogue.
keyPoints: Two-way feedback (progress at start, session value at end) is a principal contributor to implementation (Lambert).
Dorner: successful project managers review progress and correct course often.
Gilbert: improved information builds competence.
Confirmatory feedback = on course; corrective feedback = off course plus how to get back.
Principles: caring, specific, behavioural, moderate doses, dialogue, explore upside of change and downside of not changing.
Box 14.1 lists self-questions for implementing plans.

sections.heading: The Checklist
sections.detailed:
Checklists in life. People who let checklists rule their lives are the butt of many jokes; one obsessive artist even made a list of his lists. Yet Gawande (2010) showed that checklists reduced medical errors in hospitals and saved thousands of lives, and argued for their value in many other areas.

Use and misuse. Gawande has critics (Howard, 2010), and overuse of checklists can be stultifying. Howard cautions that checklists can block creativity, because clients thinking about a checklist may not be focused on solving the problem. Egan reads this as a warning that misuse or overuse of any method is self-defeating.

In therapy. To-do lists can help clients move into action, stay the course and even change course when necessary. A to-do list reminds clients of the importance of action and progress. Clients who stay in the driver's seat use to-do lists rather than become captives of them.
sections.simple: Checklists cut medical errors (Gawande) and to-do lists can help clients act and stay on track. Overused, they can block creativity (Howard). Clients should use lists, not be ruled by them.
keyPoints: Gawande (2010): checklists reduced hospital errors and saved lives.
Howard (2010): checklists can get in the way of creativity.
Misuse or overuse of any method is self-defeating.
To-do lists help clients start, persist and change course; clients should stay in the driver's seat.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Implementing Change: Helpers as Reluctant Agents of Change
sections.detailed:
Why clients fail to act. Change programmes have a large shadow side. Of the many reasons clients fail to act for themselves, Egan discusses three: helpers without an action mentality, client inertia and client entropy. He reminds readers that "implementation intentions," discussed earlier, can play an important role in managing these shadow-side obstacles.

Helper passivity. Driscoll (1984) discussed helpers' temptation to answer client passivity with passivity of their own, a "sorry, it's up to you" stance, which he called a mistake. A client who refuses responsibility invites the therapist to take over; by staying passive, the therapist refuses the invitation, forcing the client either to take initiative or endure silence. This avoids accepting the wrong kind of responsibility, but as a long-run approach it is generally ineffective. Passivity leaves the client feeling unsupported and weakens an already fragile alliance. Troubled clients are often not just unwilling but unable to take appropriate responsibility, so a passive countermove leaves both stranded in mutual inactivity with no solutions.

Helpers as active agents. To help others act, helpers must be agents and doers, not mere listeners and responders. The best helpers are active in sessions: they keep finding ways to enter clients' worlds, help clients become more active and own more of the change process, and help them see the need for action, both in their heads and in everyday life. They do this while holding the client-centred values of Chapter 2. They do not push reluctant clients so hard that reluctance turns into resistance, but neither do they sit waiting for clients to act. Box 14.2 adds that helpers must come to grips with becoming agents of change in their own lives.
sections.simple: Clients fail to act for many reasons; Egan highlights passive helpers, client inertia and entropy. Answering a passive client with passivity leaves both stuck. Good helpers are active agents who encourage action without pushing so hard that reluctance becomes resistance.
keyPoints: Three shadow-side reasons for failure to act: passive helpers, client inertia, client entropy.
Implementation intentions help manage shadow-side obstacles.
Driscoll: a passive 'it's up to you' stance leaves clients unsupported and both parties stuck.
Helpers must be agents and doers, not mere listeners and responders.
Don't push reluctance into resistance, but don't wait passively either.

sections.heading: Client Inertia: Reluctance to Get Started
sections.detailed:
What inertia is. Inertia is the human tendency to put off problem-managing action. Egan sometimes tells inertia-prone clients that the main reason sound action programmes fail is that they are never tried, that reluctance to take first steps is natural, and that they should ask what they can do to get past that initial barrier. Sources range from pure sloth to paralysing fear, and we need only look at ourselves to understand it. Egan examines passivity, learned helplessness, disabling self-talk, vicious circles and disorganisation.

Passivity. A major ingredient in the "psychopathology of the average," passivity is people's failure to take responsibility for themselves in areas of life or situations that call for action. It takes forms such as doing nothing, uncritically accepting others' goals and solutions, acting aimlessly, and becoming paralysed - shutting down or blowing up violently (Schiff, 1975). Zelda and Jerzy noticed small signs of trouble in their relationship but did nothing; lacking communication skills, they let unmanaged problems build into blowups until they ended their marriage. Little things become big things.

Learned helplessness. Seligman's concept and its link to depression matter here. Some clients learn early that they can do nothing about certain situations; feelings range from "I'm not up to this" to total helplessness with deep depression. Learned helplessness is a step beyond passivity. Bennett and Bennett (1984) saw a positive side: if problems really are beyond clients' control, an illusory sense of control, unjust self-blame and excessive expectations do not help; challenging clients' tendency to blame themselves for everything actually fostered realistic hope and change. The trick is helping clients learn what is and is not in their control - a man with a disability cannot change the disability but can control how he views it and pursue goals despite it. The opposite of helplessness is learned optimism and resourcefulness; if helplessness can be learned, so can resourcefulness, a principal goal of helping. Yet optimism is not an unmixed blessing (Chang, 2001): optimists live longer and succeed more, but pessimists predict outcomes better. Egan suggests helping clients become hopeful realists.

Disabling self-talk. Clients talk themselves into passivity with statements like "I can't do it," "I can't cope," "It's too hard," "It won't work." Such self-talk gets people into trouble and keeps them there; helpers add value by helping clients challenge it.

Vicious circles. Pyszczynski and Greenberg (1987) proposed that people whose actions fail can lose self-worth and get caught in a cycle of guilt and depression: constant self-focus intensifies negative feelings, self-derogation and negative outcomes; a negative self-image can even take on value by explaining one's plight and preventing further disappointment, and the self-focusing style maintains the depression. Amanda, enthusiastic but unaware of her company's "gentleman's club" politics, kept failing to advance, began making mistakes, talked constantly about being stuck and alienated friends. Her counsellor targeted the whole circle (low self-esteem producing passivity producing lower self-esteem), not just her self-talk, helping her become a better problem solver. Small successes started a "benign" circle of success, self-esteem and greater effort.

Disorganisation. Tico lived out of his chaotic car and never got his career, family or love life in order; disorganisation was his way of postponing life decisions. Ferguson (1987) described how innumerable little hassles distract us from asking whether we have the wrong job or mate, and how putting off important projects protects us from possible disappointment, letting us avoid adult challenges. Fear of success may lie behind it. Driscoll (1984) saw inertia as a form of control: telling clients to take the driver's seat works only until the road gets rough; better to show them they have been in the driver's seat all along. Staying disorganised is itself a successful form of control; once clients recognise their power, helpers can help redirect it.
sections.simple: Inertia is putting off action. It shows up as passivity, learned helplessness, negative self-talk, vicious circles of failure and low self-esteem, and disorganisation. Helpers help clients see what they can control, challenge self-defeating talk, create small successes and redirect the control they already exercise.
keyPoints: Inertia = tendency to put off action; sound programmes fail mostly because they are never tried.
Passivity (Schiff): doing nothing, uncritical acceptance, aimlessness, paralysis or blowing up.
Learned helplessness (Seligman) vs learned optimism and resourcefulness; aim for hopeful realists (Chang).
Disabling self-talk keeps clients passive; helpers help challenge it.
Vicious circles (Pyszczynski & Greenberg): break them with small successes into a benign circle (Amanda).
Disorganisation (Tico, Ferguson) as avoidance; Driscoll: inertia is a form of control to be redirected.

sections.heading: Entropy: The Tendency of Things to Fall Apart
sections.detailed:
What entropy is. Entropy is the tendency to slow down and abandon action already begun. Kirschenbaum (1987) calls this "self-regulatory failure." Even programmes that start strongly often dwindle: we plan, start enthusiastically, hit tedium, obstacles and complications, become discouraged, flounder, recover, flounder again and give up, telling ourselves we did not want the goals anyway.

False hopes. Polivy and Herman (2002), using dieting as their reference, describe "false hopes of self-change," with clients' unrealistic expectations at the centre, as with New Year's resolutions; this may even be the norm in self-change. Fletcher (2003), Lowe (2003) and Snyder and Rand (2003) vigorously challenged their findings and the concept, saying they paint an overly pessimistic picture. Egan notes that hope and expectancy are key ingredients of therapy, but substantive change is hard work and even true hope can fade under adversity. Expectancy helps only when it is realistic; helpers should encourage true hopes and help clients challenge false ones. Even if the research is flawed, something about it rings true.

Discretionary change. The track record of discretionary change - change not forced in some way - is poor for individuals and institutions alike. Even if change is not truly discretionary, people may perceive it so; if we think we don't have to change, we often don't, despite saying we want to. Egan's "Okavango-Kalahari phenomenon": floodwaters that turn the Okavango Delta into a wonderland vanish into the Kalahari desert, just as vigorous change programmes in organisations vanish. Helpers should ask how much of a client's change is discretionary. "Forewarned is forearmed" is realism, not pessimism.

The decay curve. Phillips (1987) identified a "ubiquitous decay curve" in helping and medical care: attrition, noncompliance and relapse are the norm. A couple reinventing their marriage may find ingrained patterns so hard to change that motivation wanes. Wise helpers accept the decay curve as part of life, warning clients that enthusiasm naturally wanes and asking what they need to keep at the task.

Lapse versus relapse. Brownell and associates (1986) drew a fine line between preparing clients for mistakes and giving them "permission" by implying mistakes are inevitable: preparation, yes; permission, no. They distinguished a lapse (a slip in an action programme) from a relapse (giving up the programme entirely). Graham, working on an angry interpersonal style with self-monitoring and self-control techniques, occasionally loses his temper but never extremely, and does not let lapses become relapse.
sections.simple: Entropy is the tendency for change efforts to fizzle out. Unrealistic 'false hopes', change that feels optional, and the natural decay curve all contribute. Helpers prepare clients for slips without giving permission, and help them keep a lapse from becoming a relapse.
keyPoints: Entropy = slowing down and giving up action begun; Kirschenbaum's 'self-regulatory failure'.
Polivy and Herman: false hopes of self-change from unrealistic expectations; critics call this too pessimistic.
Discretionary change has a poor track record (Okavango-Kalahari phenomenon).
Phillips: the ubiquitous decay curve - attrition, noncompliance and relapse.
Brownell: preparation for mistakes, yes; permission, no. A lapse need not become a relapse.

sections.heading: Resilience: People's Ability to Hold Themselves Together, Bounce Back, and Grow
sections.detailed:
Juliana's story. Egan illustrates resilience with Juliana, headstrong from the start. In college she got into drugs and drug-using boyfriends, a lifestyle that continued with changing jobs and partners. Her loving parents kept supporting her, but she "played them like a harp," and their support let her continue. After counselling they cut her loose, painfully. Things got worse and she ended up in jail, which became the turning point: she almost quit drugs, though her headstrong nature kept costing her jobs. Shaken when her father lost his job, and with minimal family contact restored, she saw a counsellor again.

Hidden inner resources. The counsellor recognised her resources: headstrong but gutsy, poor at relationships but with keen understanding of human nature, her spark intact. She secured and kept a job she liked, was promoted, made a home for her two children who had been with relatives, adopted the values of self-discipline and decency they had learned in foster homes, reconnected fully with her family and became a caring companion to her partner - rejoining the community she had abandoned.

The counsellor's role. The counsellor was a catalyst, but Juliana did the work. He encouraged her to tap the resilience or hardiness (Khoshaba & Maddi; Maddi) or growth-through-adversity (Joseph & Linley) inside her. She moved from self-loathing to non-indulgent self-esteem, success at work spread to relationships, and she became a crusader for hard work, self-discipline and avoiding self-pity. Even in the most difficult cases some residue of resilience probably remains; tapping it is the challenge.

Staying the course. Whether Juliana will stay the course is uncertain, though her achievements feel permanent. There is a literature on helping clients stay the course (e.g. Meichenbaum & Turk; Witkiewitz & Marlatt), and the literature on terminating psychotherapy offers helpful guidelines. Juliana relied on her revived strengths and social support, mainly from family; she was lucky because her family communicated well. Many would-be supporters are poor communicators who either support badly or keep their support buried inside (Cohen, Underwood & Gotlieb; Goldsmith).
sections.simple: Juliana went from drugs and jail to a stable job, a home for her children and restored family ties. Her counsellor acted as a catalyst, helping her tap resilience she still had inside. Even the hardest cases usually keep some resilience.
keyPoints: Juliana's case shows resilience surviving years of drug use and a jail term.
The counsellor was a catalyst; the client did the work.
Resilience/hardiness (Khoshaba & Maddi) or growth-through-adversity (Joseph & Linley).
Success in one area (work) spread to others (relationships).
Literature on staying the course and on terminating psychotherapy offers guidelines; supporters need communication skills.

sections.heading: Help Clients Tap into Their Resilience
sections.detailed:
Resilience under despair. Resilience can be found even in very desperate clients, though buried under despair. There has been a "mini-explosion" of theory and research on it (for example Bonanno; Reivich & Shatte; Tugade & Fredrickson), and the American Psychological Association launched a "resilience initiative" (Kersting; Newman).

Definition. Newman defines resilience as the human ability to adapt in the face of tragedy, trauma, adversity, hardship and ongoing significant life stressors.

Sources. For basic common sense, Egan points readers to the APA Help Center's "The Road to Resilience"; a full internet search would overwhelm. Glicken (2006) first tried to catalogue the attributes of resilience but, realising how far research has to go, let examples of resilience speak for themselves.
sections.simple: Even very desperate clients have some resilience buried inside. Newman defines resilience as adapting in the face of trauma, adversity and ongoing stress. Research is growing, but examples often say more than lists of traits.
keyPoints: Resilience exists even in desperate clients, buried under despair.
A 'mini-explosion' of resilience research; APA launched a resilience initiative.
Newman's definition: adapting to tragedy, trauma, adversity, hardship and ongoing stressors.
Glicken let examples speak because the science is still young.

sections.heading: Outcome Versus Process Resilience
sections.detailed:
Two kinds. Bouncing back is an essential life capability. Holaday and McPhearson (1997) compiled common factors influencing resilience; though they studied severe-burn survivors, their ideas apply to everyone. Resilience in general is the ability to overcome or adapt to significant stress or adversity. Outcome resilience implies a return to a previous state - "bounce back" resilience. Dora goes through divorce and within months is her old self, "older and wiser." Process resilience is the continuous effort to cope that is a normal part of some people's lives. Burn survivors described it as their spirit, something already deep inside that must be used, and as requiring determination, courage, struggle and choice.

Encouraging outcome resilience: Kerry. Kerry's spendthrift tendency and poor decisions put him in a financial mess. A financial counsellor who understood resilience helped him review his mistakes and guided him along a painful two-year recovery, helping him resist the temptation of bankruptcy by reviewing its consequences and talking through his low moods. Once back on his feet, they worked on prevention, given a society that idolises the super-rich. A strict budget stabilised things, and the pain of the mess kept him on the straight and narrow.

Process resilience: Oscar and Nadia. Oscar finds controlling his anger a constant struggle and must keep finding the resources to keep going. Nadia, a middle-aged single woman with chronic fatigue syndrome, digs deep daily to find the will to go on. Like many with the condition, she wants to do her best and make a good impression (Albrecht & Wallace, 1998). On good days people cannot believe she is ill - a two-edged sword: painful that intelligent people fail to notice, yet a victory that she presents her best face to the world.
sections.simple: Outcome resilience means bouncing back to how you were before, like Dora after divorce or Kerry after his money mess. Process resilience is the ongoing daily effort to cope, like Oscar with anger or Nadia with chronic fatigue. Helpers can encourage both.
keyPoints: Holaday and McPhearson studied burn survivors; findings apply to all.
Resilience = ability to overcome or adapt to significant stress or adversity.
Outcome resilience = return to a previous state ('bounce back'): Dora, Kerry.
Process resilience = continuous effort to cope as part of normal life: Oscar, Nadia.
Helpers can encourage both, including prevention after recovery.

sections.heading: Factors Contributing to Resilience
sections.detailed:
Core factors and dispositions. Holaday and McPhearson (1997) name social support, cognitive skills and psychological resources as core factors. Protective personality characteristics include an internal locus of control, empathy, curiosity, novelty seeking, a high activity level, flexibility in new situations, a sense of humour, the ability to elicit positive regard from others, accurate and positive self-appraisal, personal integrity, self-protectiveness, pride in accomplishments and a capacity for fun.

Examples. Social support: a burn victim's wife refused to let him give up and made him learn to walk again; helpers should help clients identify, create and tap into support. Fantasy and hope: fantasy can distract clients from misery so they use their resources; a client who had once managed back pain through fantasy wanted to use it again for the psychological pain of losing his fiancee, and a marine who lost both legs vowed to run again and did. A "belligerent style" (Zimrin, 1986) rather than passive enduring or yielding often aids resilience: Geraldine, a "pleasant" woman whose husband left her, became assertive, fighting for her rights without trampling others', and built a new life even though some friends found the "new" her hard. Discussing feelings: a burn survivor accepted that an occasional self-pitying bad day was OK. Avoiding self-blame and using anger's energy to cope with the world rather than damage the self: a man burned as a child stopped apologising for his scars. Personal control and interpretation: a client who got drunk for a couple of days called it "a glitch, not a pattern" and largely controlled alcohol rather than the reverse.

No scientific list yet. Resilience is not always pretty. Different researchers name different factors (Van Vliet, 2008), and there is not yet a scientific set. But the literature and life suggest every client has a range of "resilience levers"; the helper's job is to help clients discover and pull them to bounce back. Resilience is deep inside clients, part of their self-healing nature, and the communication skills described in the book are essential for tapping it.
sections.simple: Resilience is helped by social support, thinking skills and psychological resources, plus traits like humour, curiosity and an internal locus of control. Examples include using hope and fantasy, becoming more assertive, talking about feelings, avoiding self-blame and seeing setbacks as glitches. Every client has 'resilience levers' to pull.
keyPoints: Core factors (Holaday & McPhearson): social support, cognitive skills, psychological resources.
Protective dispositions include internal locus of control, empathy, curiosity, humour, flexibility, integrity, capacity for fun.
Examples: support, fantasy and hope, a 'belligerent style' (Zimrin), discussing feelings, avoiding self-blame, personal control.
No scientific set of factors yet (Van Vliet).
Every client has 'resilience levers'; communication skills help tap them.

sections.heading: Posttraumatic Growth
sections.detailed:
Beyond bouncing back. A growing literature on posttraumatic growth (Calhoun & Tedeschi; Joseph; Joseph & Linley; Tedeschi & Calhoun) concerns growth that is related to outcome resilience but goes beyond it.

Research. Phillips and Daniluk (2004), studying seven adult women sexually abused as children, found a strong sense of resiliency and growth running throughout the interviews; one woman said that without the abuse she might never have learned how unlimited the human spirit is. Bogar and Hulse-Killacky (2006), studying ten such women, identified "resiliency determinants" (being interpersonally skilled, competent, having high self-regard, being spiritual, and helpful life circumstances) and "resiliency processes" (coping strategies, refocusing and moving on, active healing, and achieving closure). Park, Lechner, Antoni and Stanton (2009) edited a book showing how medical illness can lead to positive life change.

Caution. Research on growth in abused children is socially and culturally tricky, and a large controversy erupted early in this century. Stephen Joseph (2009) advises that therapists be aware of the potential for positive change after adversity but avoid implying that trauma is inherently positive; following Tedeschi and Calhoun, growth originates not from the event but from within the person, through struggling with the event and its aftermath. Some clients can use horror as a stimulus for growth, and helpers can support them in that struggle.
sections.simple: Posttraumatic growth is positive change after trauma that goes beyond simply bouncing back. Studies of women abused as children found resilience and growth. But the growth comes from the person's struggle, not from the trauma itself, so helpers must never imply trauma is good.
keyPoints: Posttraumatic growth is related to outcome resilience but goes beyond it.
Phillips and Daniluk: resiliency and growth ran through abuse survivors' stories.
Bogar and Hulse-Killacky: resiliency determinants and resiliency processes.
Park et al.: medical illness can lead to positive life change.
Joseph: growth comes from the person's struggle, not the trauma; don't imply trauma is positive.

sections.heading: Getting Along Without a Helper: A Striking Case
sections.detailed:
Ending helping. This section carries Egan's view of how helping ends. He knows people who have stayed "in therapy" for years but says he does not understand why. He does understand several ways clients may use therapy: (1) the counsellor helps with plans, then clients take responsibility and pursue them on their own initiative and resources; (2) clients see a helper regularly during implementation until changes are "in place," then maintain them with their own internal and external resources; (3) after time with a helper, clients join a self-help group for the support needed to continue, perhaps with an occasional one-to-one session; (4) clients see a helper occasionally as need arises; (5) some clients with debilitating conditions such as bipolar or addiction disorders need to tap into therapy throughout their lives. In the end, however, most clients need to get on with their lives without a helper.

The shadow side of continuing. Some helpers enter a covert conspiracy with clients to maintain the relationship, so that talking replaces life-enhancing outcomes. The co-dependent helping relationship then becomes the problem rather than the solution. Box 14.2 accordingly lists "prepare clients to get along without a helper" as a guideline, and earlier Egan notes the literature on terminating psychotherapy offers helpful guidelines.

Vicky's case. Many problems are managed or coped with, not solved. Vicky, who certainly did not choose not to change, shows a no-formula approach. Diagnosed about 20 years earlier with manic-depressive (bipolar) disorder, she cycled through about six weeks high, six weeks low and eight weeks normal, with many hospital trips. Seven years in, she declared she would never go back to hospital and would manage her life to make hospitalisation unnecessary - a nonnegotiable goal and manifesto. In terms of Stage II Task B she spelled out what she wanted: channel the energy of her highs; consistently manage or endure her lows; not disrupt others' lives; and make no important decisions when high or low. With some help from a nontraditional counsellor, she used these broad goals to direct everything.

Her strategies. She learned all she could about her illness, including crisis cues. She channelled excess energy into useful or harmless activity, especially long phone conversations spread across many friends so no one was overburdened - her "safety valve," worth far more than avoiding a hospital stay - and she even set up a phone-answering business. She tired herself out to get the sleep she knew was essential, including working longer shifts, exercised daily, built a supportive cadre including her husband (careful not to overburden him), and used a drop-in crisis centre occasionally while avoiding anything reminiscent of hospital.

The lesson. Vicky's decision to stay out of hospital drove everything; urgency became central. Her case exemplifies the spirit of action of the implementation stage: with only occasional counselling she took charge of her life, turned her disorder into an asset, set simple goals and strategies, never looked back and was never hospitalised again. She was not "cured," but her goal was a life as normal as possible, not cure. Her approach may lack elegance, but not results. She seized life.
sections.simple: Egan believes most clients should eventually get on with life without a helper, and lists several ways clients use and leave therapy. Helpers who quietly keep clients dependent turn the relationship into the problem. Vicky, with bipolar disorder and only occasional counselling, set simple goals, used simple strategies and never went back to hospital.
keyPoints: Five patterns: plan then go solo; continue until change is in place; move to a self-help group; occasional sessions as needed; lifelong therapy for debilitating conditions.
In the end most clients need to get on with their lives without a helper.
Shadow side: covert conspiracy to maintain the relationship; co-dependent helping becomes the problem.
Vicky's nonnegotiable goal to stay out of hospital drove simple goals and strategies.
Her aim was a normal life, not cure; urgency and determination produced results.

sections.heading: Choosing Not to Change
sections.detailed:
The client's choice. Some clients analyse problems well, set goals and even identify reasonable strategies, yet effectively say that, although they understand themselves and what they need to do, they do not want to pay the price of action right now; the price of more effective living is too high.

Motivation remains a puzzle. Human motivation seems as enigmatic now as at the dawn of history. We often choose our own misery and stew in it rather than endure the relatively short-lived pain of behavioural change. Helpers can and should invite clients to challenge themselves to search for incentives and rewards for managing their lives better, and should help them understand the consequences of not changing. But in the end it is the client's choice.

Savvy helpers. This shadow side contrasts starkly with Vicky. Savvy helpers are not magicians, but they understand the shadow side of change, learn to spot its signs in each case and, in line with the values of Chapter 2, do what they can to invite clients to challenge themselves to deal with the shadow side of themselves and their world.

Box 14.2: Action-arrow guidelines for implementing change. Understand how widespread inertia and entropy are and how they affect this client; help clients become effective tacticians; help them form implementation intentions, especially when obstacles are foreseen; help them avoid both procrastination and imprudent action; help them develop contingency plans; help them discover and manage obstacles; help them discover resources to begin, persist and accomplish goals; help them find incentives and rewards to persevere; help them acquire needed skills; help them develop a social support and challenge system in daily life; prepare clients to get along without a helper; come to grips with the fact that helpers need to be agents of change in their own lives; and face up to the fact that not every client wants to change.
sections.simple: Some clients understand their problems and know what to do but decide the price of change is too high. Helpers should invite them to look for incentives and see the costs of not changing, but in the end the choice is the client's. Box 14.2 sums up the chapter's action guidelines.
keyPoints: Some clients decide the price of action is too high, despite good insight and plans.
We often choose our own misery over the short-lived pain of change.
Helpers invite clients to find incentives and see consequences of not changing; the final choice is the client's.
Savvy helpers understand the shadow side of change but are not magicians.
Box 14.2 lists 13 action-arrow guidelines, ending with 'not every client wants to change'.

sections.heading: Revisiting the Key Ingredients of Successful Therapy
sections.detailed:
Master the basics. Egan says the book is not the last word on therapy; it is contemporary, avoids fads and focuses on the basics of successful therapy. His message: become expert in the basics, then spend your career augmenting them with the best of clinical research and practice. Choose any approach, but let the basics permeate its structure and delivery.

The basics. The Client: helping is first and foremost about the client; everything the helping industry creates should serve client needs, client needs should arbitrate professional disputes, and befriending diversity is key. The Therapist: let the basics permeate your life, not just your practice; helping is not theatre, so be genuine; subordinate the profession's excesses to client needs; you do not have a success rate, clients do. The Helping Relationship: make each interaction a learning event and invest what you learn in the next client; collaboration is at the heart of the relationship. Communication Skills: prize, develop and make them second nature; use them in public and private life, teach them to your children, make dialogue your default. Feedback: make it part of every session - on between-session progress and on each session's helpfulness - and do not deny clients the chance to challenge themselves. The Treatment Approach: understand its role in the whole process; it is not the most important part, but understanding and commitment matter; choose one you can easily communicate to clients; helping is a journey taken together, not something done to clients. Problem Management: you may adopt Egan's version, but every approach involves its basics; it is not an add-on and should permeate your life. Decision Making: become expert in its dynamics and shadow side, since you make decisions throughout helping and coach clients in theirs; practise it in everyday life. The Beliefs-Values-Norms-Ethics-Morality Factors: they permeate life and helping, form the heart of social and personal culture and drive behaviour; know how they shape your life and help clients see how they drive theirs; ethics is often taught as an add-on, but should not be.

Living with uncertainty. Each ingredient brings uncertainties. Uncertainties bedevil the social sciences and the practices that flow from them, such as social work and therapy. Science seeks certainty, but therapy deals with uncertainty daily, so helpers should get comfortable being professional jugglers.
sections.simple: Egan ends by urging helpers to master the basics and build on them for life. The basics are the client, the therapist, the relationship, communication skills, feedback, the treatment approach, problem management, decision making and beliefs-values-ethics. Therapy is full of uncertainty, so helpers must become comfortable jugglers.
keyPoints: Become expert in the basics, then augment them throughout your career.
Client first; therapist genuine; collaboration at the heart of the relationship.
Communication skills and feedback in every session are essential.
Treatment approach matters but is not most important; problem management and decision making permeate all.
Beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality drive behaviour; ethics is not an add-on.
Therapy deals with uncertainty daily; become a professional juggler.

terms.definition: The phase of helping in which clients actually carry out their plans; Stages I-III plan for change, implementation is change itself.
The part of the helping model (Figure 14.1) stressing that problem-managing action should start immediately, continue throughout helping and lead to preferred outcomes.
Kanfer and Schefft's term for self-control in which a single choice ends a conflict, e.g. deciding to leave an abusive spouse and doing it.
Kanfer and Schefft's term for self-control requiring continued resistance to temptation over time, needing a preventive mentality and street smarts.
A practical plan or programme for accomplishing an objective.
The art of adapting a plan to the immediate situation, including changing it on the spot to handle unforeseen complications.
The art of providing the resources needed to implement a plan in a timely way.
The age-old gap between knowing what to do and doing it (Kegan & Lahey; Pfeffer & Sutton).
Kegan and Lahey's term for unacknowledged commitments that block change, e.g. a principal's belief that authority figures should stay on a pedestal.
Kegan and Lahey's term for each person's set of factors that keep him or her from changing.
Andreou's term for procrastinating on implementing a solution to procrastination itself, avoiding the most critical actions (Eula).
Kotter's term for doing the right things in a timely way; needed for change to start, continue and stick.
Kotter's term for lots of activity, even frenzied, that looks like urgency but goes nowhere.
Partnoy's idea that delaying decisions and actions can give time to think about consequences, especially of acting too quickly.
Acting rashly, such as rushing to try the first strategy that comes to mind, often based on flawed assumptions (Elmer).
Lewin's method: a client's review of the major obstacles to (restraining forces) and facilitating forces for implementing action plans; 'forewarned is forearmed'.
Pitfalls to implementing a programme, arising from within clients, from others, from social settings and from larger environmental forces.
Unused or available resources that help clients act, e.g. Nora's Bible reading or George taking a friend along.
Deep, substantive change; Mara's three intersecting goals each involved it and together constituted massive second-order change.
What drives action; clients avoid programmes when incentives for not acting outweigh those for acting, and incentives need tending.
