Tasks Miguel's counsellor had him devise at home, on the beat and with friends to experience the rewards of decency.
Additional incentives developed for times when current incentives lose their power (Dwight).
The process by which constructive-change activities that are not rewarded lose vigour, decrease and disappear (Luigi).
An agreement clients make with themselves (and sometimes others) that focuses energy on initiating and sustaining action.
Karlan's approach (stickK): setting a goal, putting stakes at risk, an objective referee, supporters and transparency.
Help from people in clients' lives; one of the most important resources, effective only if perceived as supportive by the client.
Putnam's term for informal social connectedness and formal civic engagement, which has fallen in North American society.
Enlisting the help of friends in a change effort; energising, unlike dependence, which limits and depresses (Wing & Jeffery).
Relationships providing a judicious mixture of encouragement and challenge; support without challenge is hollow, challenge without support abrasive.
The people with whom one discusses important matters; many Americans have none (McPherson, Smith-Lovin & Brashears).
Feedback on progress toward outcomes at the start of each session and on the value of the session at the end; a principal contributor to implementation.
Feedback from significant others telling clients they are on course toward a goal.
Feedback telling clients they have wandered off course and specifying what they need to do to get back on.
A tool that helps clients move into action, stay the course and change course; useful unless overused or misused.
Specific plans for action, discussed earlier in the book, that help manage shadow-side obstacles, especially foreseen ones.

terms.term: Helpers as reluctant agents of change
terms.definition: Helpers who respond to client passivity with their own passive 'it's up to you' stance (Driscoll), leaving both stuck.
The human tendency to put off problem-managing action; sources range from sloth to paralysing fear.
Failure to take responsibility for oneself where action is called for; forms include doing nothing, uncritical acceptance, aimlessness and paralysis or blowing up (Schiff).
Everyday dysfunction in ordinary people, of which passivity is a major ingredient.
Seligman's concept: learning that nothing can be done about certain situations; linked with depression and a step beyond passivity.
Seligman's term for the opposite of helplessness; along with resourcefulness, it can be learned.
Egan's suggested aim for clients: neither naive optimists nor pessimists.
Self-defeating inner statements ('I can't do it', 'It won't work') that talk clients into passivity.
Pyszczynski and Greenberg's cycle in which failure leads to lost self-worth, self-focus, guilt and depression, which produce further failure.
A positive cycle in which small successes raise self-esteem, leading to greater efforts to succeed (Amanda).
Keeping life chaotic as a way of putting off important decisions and challenges (Tico; Ferguson).
Driscoll's view that staying disorganised is itself a successful form of control which clients can learn to redirect.
The tendency to slow down and give up action that has been initiated.
Kirschenbaum's term for the dwindling of self-change efforts.
Polivy and Herman's syndrome in which unrealistic expectations lead to repeated failed self-change attempts.
Change that is not forced; its track record in individuals and institutions is poor.
Egan's image for change programmes that start vigorously but disappear, like floodwaters vanishing into the desert.
Phillips's 'ubiquitous decay curve': attrition, noncompliance and relapse in helping and medical care.
A slip or mistake in an action programme that need not lead to giving it up (Brownell).
Giving up an action programme entirely (Brownell).
Newman: the human ability to adapt in the face of tragedy, trauma, adversity, hardship and ongoing significant stressors.
'Bounce back' resilience implying a return to a previous state (Holaday & McPhearson).
The continuous effort to cope that is a normal part of some people's lives (Holaday & McPhearson).
Zimrin's term for an active, fighting coping style that contributes more to resilience than passive enduring or yielding.
Egan's term for the range of resilience resources in every client that helpers help them discover and pull.
Positive change after trauma, related to but going beyond outcome resilience; it originates from the person's struggle, not the event.
Bogar and Hulse-Killacky: interpersonally skilled, competent, high self-regard, spiritual, helpful life circumstances.
Bogar and Hulse-Killacky: coping strategies, refocusing and moving on, active healing, achieving closure.
A covert conspiracy between helper and client to maintain the relationship, in which talking replaces outcomes and the relationship becomes the problem.
A client's decision, despite insight and plans, that the price of action is too high; ultimately the client's choice.

studies.title: Kirschenbaum (1987): why change fails
studies.finding: Low commitment, weak self-efficacy, poor outcome expectations, self-punishment, depressive thinking, poor stress coping, inconsistent self-monitoring, poor habit-change techniques, social pressure, failure to cope with initial relapse and focusing on difficulty all contribute to not starting or giving up.

studies.title: Sherman and associates (2008): support for veterans with PTSD
studies.finding: Families, spouses and friends hold back for many reasons (not enlisted, distance, beliefs, reluctance, fear; hopelessness, resignation, focus on children), showing support must be actively enrolled.

studies.title: Karlan (2008): commitment contracts
studies.finding: Goals, stakes at risk, a referee, supporters and public commitment (stickK) help people move forward and make giving up harder.

studies.title: NAMHC Task Force (1996): social support and mental illness
studies.finding: In about 75% of studies of clinically depressed patients, support improved initial treatment success and maintenance; in schizophrenia and alcoholism, more support meant fewer relapses and hospitalisations.

studies.title: NAMHC Task Force: distress and support
studies.finding: Highly distressed people, who most need support, may be least likely to get it because their distress drives supporters away.

studies.title: Putnam (2000): social capital
studies.finding: Informal connectedness and civic engagement have fallen in North America.

studies.title: Wing and Jeffery (1999): weight loss
studies.finding: Clients who enlisted friends were much more successful at losing weight and maintaining the loss than those going solo.

studies.title: McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Brashears (2006): confidants
studies.finding: Many people in the US have no one to confide in, confirming that Americans increasingly 'bowl alone'.

studies.title: Dorner (1996): project managers
studies.finding: Successful project managers reviewed progress, looked for unintended consequences and corrected course often.

studies.title: Gawande (2010): checklists
studies.finding: Checklists reduced medical errors in hospitals and saved thousands of lives.

studies.title: Bennett and Bennett (1984): helplessness
studies.finding: Challenging clients' tendency to blame themselves for everything fostered realistic hope and change.

studies.title: Chang (2001): optimism
studies.finding: Optimists live longer and succeed more, but pessimists are better predictors of what will happen.

studies.title: Polivy and Herman (2002): false hopes
studies.finding: Unrealistic expectations produce repeated failure in self-change such as dieting; critics (Fletcher, Lowe, Snyder & Rand) called this overly pessimistic.

studies.title: Phillips (1987): decay curve
studies.finding: Attrition, noncompliance and relapse are pervasive in helping and medical care.

studies.title: Brownell and associates (1986): lapse and relapse
studies.finding: A lapse need not become a relapse; prepare clients for mistakes without giving permission.

studies.title: Holaday and McPhearson (1997): burn survivors
studies.finding: Distinguished outcome and process resilience; core factors are social support, cognitive skills and psychological resources, plus protective dispositions.

studies.title: Phillips and Daniluk (2004): adult survivors of childhood sexual abuse
studies.finding: In seven women, a strong sense of resiliency and growth ran throughout the interviews.

studies.title: Bogar and Hulse-Killacky (2006): ten abuse survivors
studies.finding: Identified resiliency determinants and resiliency processes that facilitated adult resiliency.

studies.title: Park, Lechner, Antoni and Stanton (2009)
studies.finding: Medical illness can lead to positive life change.

examples.title: Decisional vs protracted self-control in exam prep
examples.text: A student decides to delete a gaming app before exams - one decision ends the conflict (decisional). Not reinstalling it during six weeks of tempting evenings, and avoiding friends' gaming sessions in the first place, is protracted self-control.

examples.title: Strategy, tactics, logistics for a coaching class
examples.text: Plan: join a weekend coaching batch (strategy). The batch is full, so you join the weekday evening batch instead (tactics) and borrow a friend's notes and arrange a ride (logistics).

examples.title: Force-field analysis for a morning routine
examples.text: Goal: study at 6 a.m. Restraining forces: late-night phone use, a noisy household. Facilitating forces: a roommate who also wakes early, a quiet terrace. Plan to weaken the first list and use the second.

examples.title: Lapse, not relapse
examples.text: Someone quitting junk food eats samosas at a wedding. Treating it as 'a glitch, not a pattern' and going back to the plan the next day is a lapse; giving up the whole plan is a relapse.

examples.title: Confirmatory feedback done well
examples.text: Instead of 'good presentation', a guide says: 'You kept to time, used two clear examples and handled the tough question calmly - the class stayed with you.' Specific behaviour plus impact turns praise into learning.

checks.q: According to Egan, Stages I, II and III of the helping model revolve around:
options: Planning for change rather than change itself
checks.explain: Egan states that the three stages and nine tasks all concern planning for change, not change itself; the Action Arrow concerns action.

checks.q: Continued resistance to temptation, as in staying on a demanding health programme day after day, is what Kanfer and Schefft call:
checks.explain: Protracted self-control requires ongoing resistance to temptation; decisional self-control is a single choice that ends a conflict.

checks.q: What is Mara's top priority as reviewed with Carlos?
options: Developing a community of friends and colleagues
checks.explain: Mara says building a community of friends and colleagues as the basis of a social life remains her top goal; a relationship she will 'play by ear'.

checks.q: Why is Mara unsure whether 'normalising' her relationship with her parents is a goal?
options: She has no feelings about her parents
Carlos told her to drop it
Her parents have already agreed to it
It is not co-owned by her parents
checks.explain: Egan notes normalising would require all three to work together, and her father's 'case-closed' mentality blocks cooperation.

checks.q: The art of adapting a plan to the immediate situation, including changing it on the spot, is:
checks.explain: Egan defines tactics as adapting the plan to the immediate situation; strategy is the plan and logistics is timely provision of resources.

checks.q: Norcross, Krebs and Prochaska caution helpers to:
options: Always push clients into action in the first session
Beware treating all clients as though they are in action
checks.explain: They warn that most clients arrive not ready for action.

checks.q: Andreou's 'second-order procrastination' refers to:
options: Delaying twice as long as planned
Procrastinating on implementing a solution to procrastination itself
checks.explain: Eula stayed busy but avoided the critical actions, procrastinating on the solution to her procrastination.

checks.q: Kotter's 'false urgency' is best described as:
options: Doing the right things in a timely way
Delaying decisions to think about consequences
A hidden commitment that blocks change
Lots of frenzied activity that goes nowhere
checks.explain: Kotter contrasts true urgency (right things, timely) with false urgency, activity that only looks like urgency.

checks.q: Elmer's counsellor failed to help him avoid which two mistakes?
options: Setting an unrealistic goal and acting on the first strategy that came along
Relying on social support and ignoring medicine
checks.explain: Egan says Elmer aimed to be pain-free without testing realism and rushed into the first programme he found.

checks.q: When Carlos explores Mara's 'more or less' decision to tell her mother her plans, Mara concludes she must:
options: Tell her father directly at once
Rethink how to be both honest and prudent with her parents
Cut off contact with her parents
Give up her plans for the future
checks.explain: Exploring 'more or less' revealed moral doubts and unexplored fallout, so she decided to rethink.

checks.q: The slogan associated with Lewin's force-field analysis is:
checks.explain: Egan gives 'forewarned is forearmed' as the slogan of force-field analysis.

checks.q: How did the counsellor help Raul and Maria cope with the adoption interview?
options: Writing to the agency on their behalf
Teaching them to suppress their feelings
Role-playing a tough examiner and linking them with a mutual-help group
checks.explain: Two role-plays with a 'hard line' examiner and a mutual-help group trained them to cope with restraining forces.

checks.q: Constructive activities that are not rewarded lose vigour and disappear. This is called:
checks.explain: Egan names this process extinction and illustrates it with Luigi.

checks.q: Why did Dwight's counsellor look for 'backup' incentives?
options: Incentives that start change may lose power and not keep it going
Backup incentives replace the need for a counsellor
checks.explain: Egan notes incentives that get a client going may not keep him going, so backups are needed.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of Karlan's commitment-contract principles adaptable to therapy?
checks.explain: Karlan stresses transparency and public commitment, not secrecy.

checks.q: In the seventh-grader case, what made the contract work?
options: He valued being with classmates, so he paid the price of self-control
checks.explain: Spending a day away from friends cost him the socializing he valued, so disruptions dropped.

checks.q: Wing and Jeffery's finding that clients who enlisted friends lost more weight illustrates:
checks.explain: Egan calls this social facilitation, which energises, unlike dependence.

checks.q: According to Lakey, what has perhaps the most influence on social support?
options: The kind and quality of the client's relationship with the support provider
Objective supportive actions regardless of perception
checks.explain: Lakey stresses the relationship; support counts only if perceived as such by the client.

checks.q: Egan's view of support and challenge is that:
options: Support alone is sufficient for change
Challenge should come only from helpers
Support without challenge can be hollow, and challenge without support abrasive
Friends should never challenge an ill person
checks.explain: He calls for a judicious mixture of encouragement and challenge.

checks.q: Harry's friends helped him by:
options: Mixing support with challenge, including mocking his invalid movements
checks.explain: They mocked invalid behaviour, held serious talks, ignored symptom talk and included him in plans.

checks.q: Feedback that tells clients they have wandered off course and what to do to get back on is:
checks.explain: Egan defines corrective feedback this way; confirmatory feedback tells them they are on course.

checks.q: Which is a principle of corrective feedback listed by Egan?
options: Give as much feedback as possible at once
Focus on behaviours rather than elusive personality characteristics
checks.explain: Egan lists focusing on behaviour, moderate doses, dialogue and avoiding impatient negative language.

checks.q: Howard's criticism of checklists is that they:
options: Can stand in the way of creativity
checks.explain: Howard warns that thinking about a checklist can distract from solving the problem.

checks.q: Egan's conclusion about to-do lists in therapy is that clients should:
options: Use them rather than become captives of them
checks.explain: Clients who stay in the driver's seat use to-do lists rather than become their captives.

checks.q: Which three shadow-side reasons for failure to act does Egan discuss?
options: Helpers lacking an action mentality, client inertia and client entropy
Poor diagnosis, poor medication and poor insight
checks.explain: Egan names these three explicitly.

checks.q: Driscoll argued that a therapist's passive 'it's up to you' stance:
options: Is the most effective long-run approach
Leaves the client unsupported and both stuck in inactivity
Always forces clients to take responsibility
checks.explain: Driscoll says it is generally ineffective long term, impairs the alliance and strands both parties.

checks.q: Learned helplessness, according to Egan, is:
checks.explain: Egan describes learned helplessness as going beyond passivity, ranging up to total helplessness with depression.

checks.q: Amanda's counsellor helped break her vicious circle mainly by:
options: Advising her to quit her job
Telling her to stop talking to friends
Helping her become a better problem solver so small successes started a benign circle
checks.explain: He focused on the whole circle and her problem solving, not just inner self-talk.

checks.q: Entropy is defined in the chapter as:
options: The tendency to slow down and give up action that has been initiated
The tendency to put off starting action
Learning that nothing can be done
checks.explain: Inertia is putting off action; entropy is giving up action already begun.

checks.q: Brownell and associates' guidance about mistakes is:
checks.explain: They distinguished preparing clients for mistakes from implying mistakes are inevitable.

checks.q: What turned out to be the turning point for Juliana?
checks.explain: Egan says jail seemed to be the turning point, after which she all but quit drugs.

checks.q: In Juliana's case, the counsellor's role is described as:
checks.explain: The counsellor played a catalytic role while Juliana did the work.

checks.q: Newman defines resilience as:
options: The human ability to adapt in the face of tragedy, trauma, adversity, hardship and ongoing stressors
Returning exactly to a previous state
Growth that originates in the traumatic event
checks.explain: This is Newman's definition quoted by Egan.

checks.q: Glicken's approach to resilience was to:
options: Try to catalogue its attributes, then let examples speak for themselves
checks.explain: Realising science had far to go, Glicken let examples of resilience speak.

checks.q: Dora bouncing back to 'her old self' after divorce illustrates:
checks.explain: Outcome resilience implies return to a previous state.

checks.q: Nadia, who must dig deep every day to cope with chronic fatigue syndrome, illustrates:
checks.explain: Process resilience is the continuous effort to cope as part of normal life.

checks.q: Holaday and McPhearson's core factors influencing resilience are:
options: Social support, cognitive skills and psychological resources
checks.explain: These are the three core factors named.

checks.q: Geraldine becoming assertive after her husband left illustrates Zimrin's:
checks.explain: A belligerent rather than passively enduring style often contributes more to resilience.

checks.q: Posttraumatic growth, according to Egan, is:
options: The same as returning to a previous state
Related to outcome resilience but goes beyond it
checks.explain: Egan says it is related to outcome resilience but goes beyond it.

checks.q: Stephen Joseph, following Tedeschi and Calhoun, says growth after trauma originates from:
options: Within the person, through struggling with the event and its aftermath
checks.explain: Helpers should not imply trauma is inherently positive.

checks.q: Egan's view on ending helping is that, in the end:
options: Most clients need to get on with their lives without a helper
All clients should stay in therapy for life
Clients should never join self-help groups
Termination should be decided only by the helper
checks.explain: Egan lists ways clients use therapy but concludes most must manage without a helper.

checks.q: What drove everything in Vicky's management of her bipolar disorder?
options: Her decision never to be hospitalised again

practice.q: Discuss the principles of effective implementation that, according to Egan, help clients move from planning to action.
practice.answer:
Introduction. In Chapter 14 of The Skilled Helper, Egan points out that Stages I, II and III of the helping model are about planning for change, while the Action Arrow insists that problem-managing action should begin immediately, continue throughout helping and lead to the client's preferred outcomes. Norcross, Krebs and Prochaska warn that most clients arrive not ready for action, yet the sooner clients act the more likely they are to succeed; the helper must bridge this gap with patience, since progress is often small changes, plateaus and regressions (Johancen-Walt). Plans need strategy (a practical plan), tactics (adapting the plan to the immediate situation) and logistics (providing resources in time), as in Rebecca's switch to a cheaper community-college course. Because many motivated clients are poor tacticians, Egan offers five principles.

1. Help clients overcome procrastination. The "knowing-doing gap" is ancient. Kegan and Lahey describe hidden commitments that create a personal "immunity to change," as with a principal who avoids classrooms because authority figures should stay on a pedestal. Many clients focus on the short-term pain of acting. Eula stayed busy researching and drafting plans but finished no product, showing Andreou's second-order procrastination - putting off the solution to procrastination itself; once her counsellor helped her see her fear, she marketed a product and others followed. Kotter distinguishes true urgency (right things, timely) from false urgency (frenzied activity going nowhere), and Partnoy notes some procrastination is good because it allows reflection.

2. Help clients avoid imprudent action. Some clients rush into the first strategy they find. Elmer, with chronic back pain, signed up for a distant pain clinic without consulting anyone, expecting to become pain-free, and returned within ten days more depressed. His counsellor failed to help him avoid an unrealistic goal and a hasty strategy; action built on flawed assumptions cannot be prudent. Carlos, by contrast, helps Mara explore her "more or less" decision to tell her mother her plans, and she decides to rethink how to be honest and prudent.

3. Help clients identify obstacles and resources. Lewin's force-field analysis reviews restraining and facilitating forces: "forewarned is forearmed." Raul and Maria, planning to adopt, anticipated feeling scrutinised and frustrated by delays; role-plays and a mutual-help group prepared them. Obstacles may come from within, from others, from social settings or wider forces, and the aim is a sensible census, not a search for everything that could go wrong. Facilitating forces include Nora's Bible reading before dialysis and George bringing a friend to a feared procedure. Mara's sudden obstacle - the dealership's closure and her father's pension losses - became an opportunity and clarified three intersecting goals.

4. Help clients find incentives and rewards. Clients avoid programmes when rewards for not acting outweigh rewards for acting. Miguel's counsellor confronted him and helped him find incentives in "decency" through experiments in decency rather than relying on fear. Dwight needed backup incentives because the ones that start change may not sustain it. Unrewarded activity undergoes extinction, as with Luigi until he found more challenging work. Incentives need tending.

5. Help clients develop action-focused self-contracts. Self-contracts and agreements with others focus energy. Support must be enrolled; Sherman and associates show many reasons families fail to support veterans with PTSD. Karlan's stickK uses goals, stakes, a referee, supporters and transparency. A seventh-grader's contract involving parents, teacher and principal sharply reduced his disruptions because he valued being with classmates.

Conclusion. For Egan, implementation means helping clients act promptly and prudently, anticipate obstacles, use resources, tend incentives and commit publicly. Box 14.2 summarises these as action-arrow guidelines, including implementation intentions and contingency plans.

practice.q: Discuss termination (ending of helping) according to Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan does not treat termination as a separate technical stage. In Chapter 14 he deals with ending helping under the heading "Getting Along Without a Helper," arguing that the purpose of helping is life-enhancing outcomes in clients' real lives, not an endless relationship. Box 14.2 makes this an explicit guideline: prepare clients to get along without a helper.

Ways clients use and leave therapy. Egan says he knows people who have stayed "in therapy" for years and does not understand why. He does understand five patterns. First, the counsellor helps clients with plans and the clients then take responsibility and pursue them using their own initiative and resources. Second, clients see a helper regularly during implementation until desired changes are "in place," then maintain them with their own internal and external resources. Third, after some time with a helper, clients join a self-help group for the support needed to continue, perhaps with an occasional one-to-one session. Fourth, clients see a helper occasionally as the need arises. Fifth, some clients with debilitating conditions such as bipolar or addiction disorders need to tap into therapy throughout their lives. In the end, however, most clients need to get on with their lives without a helper.

The shadow side of not ending. Egan warns that some helpers enter a covert conspiracy with clients to maintain the relationship. Talking replaces outcomes, and the co-dependent helping relationship becomes the problem rather than the solution.

Preparing clients to manage alone. Several parts of the chapter show how clients are made ready. Mara illustrates one overall goal of helping: learning to apply problem management to problems and opportunities on her own; faced with her family's financial collapse, she arrives composed and ready to work, with Carlos acting as her consultant. Egan stresses that clients' main support should be "out there" in their lives rather than with the helper, so helpers assist clients to build social support and challenge systems and to find people who can give feedback. In Juliana's case the counsellor was a catalyst while she did the work, relying afterwards on her revived inner strengths and family support. Egan notes that the literature on helping clients stay the course and on terminating psychotherapy offers helpful guidelines, and that would-be supporters need good communication skills.

Vicky: a striking case. Vicky, diagnosed with bipolar disorder about 20 years earlier and repeatedly hospitalised, declared she would never return to hospital. She set simple goals - channel the energy of highs, manage or endure lows, avoid disrupting others, make no major decisions when high or low - and devised simple strategies: learning about her illness, long phone calls spread across friends, a phone-answering business, sleep, exercise and a supportive cadre including her husband, using a crisis centre only occasionally. With only occasional help from a nontraditional counsellor she was never hospitalised again. Her goal was a normal life, not cure.

Choosing not to change. Ending may also come when clients decide the price of change is too high. Helpers invite them to look for incentives and understand the consequences of not changing, but in the end it is the client's choice.

Conclusion. For Egan, a good ending means clients carry on problem management with their own resources and real-world support. Helpers should work toward this from the start and avoid co-dependent relationships, accepting that a few clients need ongoing or occasional help.

practice.q: Explain the shadow side of implementing change as described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan says change programmes have a large shadow side. Of the many reasons clients fail to act, he discusses three: helpers who lack an action mentality, client inertia and client entropy. Implementation intentions can help manage these obstacles.

Helpers as reluctant agents of change. Driscoll described helpers' temptation to meet client passivity with their own passivity - a "sorry, it's up to you" stance. It avoids accepting the wrong responsibility, but long term it leaves clients unsupported, weakens the fragile alliance and strands both in inactivity, especially since troubled clients are often unable, not just unwilling, to take responsibility. Egan argues helpers must be agents and doers, active in sessions, helping clients own change and see the need for action, while keeping client-centred values and not pushing reluctance into resistance.

Client inertia. Inertia is the tendency to put off action; sound programmes fail mostly because they are never tried. Its forms include:
Passivity - failure to take responsibility where action is needed, a major part of the "psychopathology of the average": doing nothing, uncritically accepting others' solutions, aimlessness, or paralysis/blowing up (Schiff). Zelda and Jerzy's unaddressed small problems ended their marriage.
Learned helplessness - Seligman's concept linked with depression, a step beyond passivity. Bennett and Bennett found challenging excessive self-blame fostered realistic hope; clients must learn what is and is not in their control. The opposite is learned optimism and resourcefulness, though Chang notes optimism has costs, so clients should be hopeful realists.
Disabling self-talk - "I can't do it," "It won't work" - which helpers help clients challenge.
Vicious circles - Pyszczynski and Greenberg's cycle of failure, self-focus, guilt and depression. Amanda's counsellor targeted the whole circle by improving her problem solving, starting a benign circle.
Disorganisation - Tico's chaotic life postponed decisions; Ferguson shows hassles distract us from big questions. Driscoll saw inertia as control: clients are already in the driver's seat and can redirect that power.

Client entropy. Entropy is the tendency to slow down and give up action begun (Kirschenbaum's self-regulatory failure). Polivy and Herman's "false hopes of self-change" rest on unrealistic expectations; critics called this too pessimistic, but Egan urges helping clients challenge false hopes and keep true ones. Discretionary change has a poor track record (the Okavango-Kalahari phenomenon). Phillips's ubiquitous decay curve shows attrition, noncompliance and relapse are common, so helpers warn clients that enthusiasm wanes. Brownell advises preparation for mistakes but not permission, and separates a lapse from a relapse, as with Graham.

Conclusion. Box 14.2 urges helpers to understand how widespread inertia and entropy are, to become agents of change themselves, and to face the fact that not every client wants to change.

practice.q: What is resilience? Discuss outcome and process resilience, factors contributing to resilience and posttraumatic growth with reference to Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan treats resilience - people's ability to hold themselves together, bounce back and grow - as a key resource in implementation. Newman defines it as the human ability to adapt in the face of tragedy, trauma, adversity, hardship and ongoing significant stressors. Research has grown rapidly and the APA launched a resilience initiative, though Glicken ended up letting examples speak for themselves.

Juliana's case. Juliana spent years with drugs and drug-using partners, exploited her parents' support, was cut loose and went to jail, which became her turning point. A counsellor recognised her hidden resources - guts, a keen understanding of human nature, her spark. She built a career, made a home for her children, reconnected with family and became a caring partner. The counsellor was a catalyst; she did the work, tapping her hardiness (Khoshaba & Maddi) or growth-through-adversity (Joseph & Linley). Even the hardest cases probably keep some residue of resilience.

Outcome versus process resilience. Holaday and McPhearson, studying severe-burn survivors, defined resilience as overcoming or adapting to significant stress. Outcome resilience implies returning to a previous state - "bounce back," as when Dora is her old self, "older and wiser," after divorce, or Kerry recovers from a financial mess over two years and then works on prevention. Process resilience is the continuous coping that is a normal part of some lives: Oscar's constant struggle with anger, or Nadia digging deep daily with chronic fatigue syndrome. Helpers can encourage both.

Factors contributing to resilience. Holaday and McPhearson name social support, cognitive skills and psychological resources, plus protective dispositions: internal locus of control, empathy, curiosity, novelty seeking, high activity, flexibility, humour, eliciting positive regard, accurate positive self-appraisal, integrity, self-protectiveness, pride in accomplishment and a capacity for fun. Examples: a wife who made her burned husband walk again (support); fantasy and hope, like the marine who said he would run again and did; Zimrin's "belligerent style," seen in Geraldine's new assertiveness; discussing feelings; avoiding self-blame and using anger's energy outward; and interpreting setbacks as "a glitch, not a pattern." There is no scientific list yet (Van Vliet), but every client has "resilience levers" that communication skills help tap.

Posttraumatic growth. This is related to outcome resilience but goes beyond it. Phillips and Daniluk found resiliency and growth in women abused as children; Bogar and Hulse-Killacky identified resiliency determinants (interpersonally skilled, competent, high self-regard, spiritual, helpful circumstances) and processes (coping strategies, refocusing and moving on, active healing, achieving closure); Park and colleagues showed illness can lead to positive change. Stephen Joseph cautions that growth comes from the person's struggle, not the trauma, so helpers must not imply trauma is inherently positive.

Conclusion. For Egan, resilience is part of clients' self-healing nature; the helper's task is to help clients discover and use it.

practice.q: Discuss the role of social support and challenge in implementing change, according to Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan regards social support as one of the most important resources clients need to pursue goals, though research on it is surprisingly skimpy, so common sense must sometimes outpace science. Lakey argues the professions still lack understanding of support processes; the client's relationship with the support provider matters most, and support counts only if the client perceives it as support.

Evidence and context. The NAMHC Task Force (1996) found support improved treatment success and maintenance in about 75% of studies with depressed patients, and was linked to fewer relapses and hospitalisations in schizophrenia and alcoholism. Helpers give support, but clients' main support should be in their real lives. Putnam shows that social capital has declined in North America. Wing and Jeffery found weight-loss clients who enlisted friends did much better - social facilitation, which energises, unlike dependence.

Two kinds of clients. Some have impoverished social lives and need help getting back into community. Others have people but use them poorly; Casey, who hid his illness to avoid being a burden, was challenged to ask local friends for help and added caring church members to his network. Highly distressed people may drive supporters away, so they can learn to modulate distress and supporters can learn to cope. Support must also be enrolled: Sherman and associates list many reasons families fail to support veterans with PTSD.

Challenging relationships. Support without challenge can be hollow; challenge without support abrasive. Harry's friends, seeing him adopt invalid behaviour, mocked it, held serious talks, ignored symptom talk and included him in plans, and he lived fully until his death. McPherson and colleagues found many Americans have no confidants; Mara realises she needs confidants beyond Carlos.

Two-way feedback. Feedback on progress at the start of each session and on the session's value at the end is a principal contributor to implementation (Lambert); Dorner found successful managers corrected course often, and Gilbert claimed better information builds competence. Confirmatory feedback tells clients they are on course; corrective feedback tells them they are off course and how to get back. Corrective feedback should be caring, specific, behavioural, moderate, dialogic, and should help clients see impact, alternatives and the upside of change. Confirmatory feedback should be equally specific, as in a father's detailed praise of his son. Box 14.1 lists self-questions for implementation.

The checklist. Gawande showed checklists save lives; Howard warns they can block creativity. To-do lists help clients act if clients stay in the driver's seat.

Conclusion. Egan sees a social support and challenge system in daily life, plus honest feedback, as central to sustained change and to clients eventually managing without a helper.

practice.q: Differentiate decisional and protracted self-control with examples.
practice.answer:
Egan draws on Kanfer and Schefft to distinguish two kinds of self-control needed in implementation.

Decisional self-control: a single choice ends a conflict. Egan's example is a woman who decides to leave an abusive spouse and goes through with it. A client deciding to give up alcohol completely is also exercising decisional self-control.

Protracted self-control: continued resistance to temptation over time. A client with serious health problems must not only start a demanding diet, exercise and stress programme but stay vigilant daily, renewing her resolve at each temptation. It helps to treat temptations as learning opportunities rather than battles and to make the struggle tolerable or rewarding, like the client who munched a carrot when tempted.

Most clients need both. The person who gives up alcohol must handle long-term temptations, which calls for a preventive mentality and street smarts - declining a bar invitation is easier than sitting in a bar all evening without drinking. In Mara's case, deciding to leave home would be decisional, but she would need protracted self-control to manage separation, guilt and early loneliness.

Egan also links self-control to Kirschenbaum's findings: low commitment, failure to cope with initial relapse and focusing on the difficulty of change rather than the attractiveness of the outcome all undermine it. Discipline and self-control, as aspects of self-responsibility, therefore play an important role in implementing any change programme.

practice.q: Explain force-field analysis and its use in helping clients implement plans.
practice.answer:
Force-field analysis was developed by Kurt Lewin, who in Egan's words codified common sense. It is a client's review of the major obstacles to (restraining forces) and the major facilitating forces for implementing action plans. Its slogan is "forewarned is forearmed."

Obstacles. Knowing likely "wrinkles" makes clients less disoriented when they arise. It should be a straightforward census of likely pitfalls, not a self-defeating search for everything that might go wrong. Obstacles may come from within clients, other people, social settings or wider environmental forces. Raul and Maria, planning to adopt, anticipated negative feelings under agency scrutiny and frustration over delays; the counsellor role-played a tough examiner and linked them to a mutual-help group. Sometimes awareness alone is enough; sometimes explicit coping strategies are needed.

Facilitating forces. Helpers also help clients find unused resources. Nora replaced "poor-me" thinking about dialysis with Bible reading and meditation; George took a friend to a feared procedure, which committed him and distracted him from fear. Brainstorming such resources raises the probability that clients act in their own interests.

Mara shows that obstacles can appear at any time: the sudden closure of the dealership and her father's pension losses were an obstacle 'with a capital O', yet she treated the crisis as opening the way to a new career and to networking. Force-field analysis thus prepares clients both to cope with pitfalls and to spot opportunities.

practice.q: Distinguish confirmatory and corrective feedback and list Egan's principles for giving corrective feedback.
practice.answer:
Egan sees feedback as a way of giving encouragement and challenge; its purpose is information, guidance, support and challenge, not judgment.

Confirmatory feedback: significant others (helpers, relatives, friends, colleagues) let clients know they are on course toward a goal.
Corrective feedback: they let clients know they have wandered off course and specify what to do to get back on.

Principles for corrective feedback: help clients give feedback to themselves; give it in a spirit of caring; treat mistakes as opportunities for growth; mix confirmatory and corrective feedback; be concrete, specific, brief and to the point; focus on behaviour, not elusive personality traits; help clients see whether behaviour helps or hinders goals; explore its impact and implications; avoid impatient negative language; give moderate doses; engage in dialogue rather than lecturing; help clients discover alternatives, suggesting if needed; and help them explore the upside of changing and downside of not changing.

The same spirit applies to confirmatory feedback: a father's specific praise of his son's stand against bullies, noting behaviour and impact, is far more powerful than "I'm proud of you."

Egan notes one main difficulty: finding people in the client's daily life who see the client in action often enough, care enough to give feedback and have the skills to give it constructively. Within therapy, two-way feedback at the start and end of each session serves the same purpose of course correction.

practice.q: How does Egan explain procrastination and how can helpers address it?
practice.answer:
Egan places procrastination within the "knowing-doing gap" (Kegan & Lahey; Pfeffer & Sutton). Kegan and Lahey describe hidden commitments that block change - a principal avoiding classrooms may be committed to keeping authority figures on a pedestal - and each person's factors create an "immunity to change." Many clients focus on the short-term pain of acting despite seeing long-term benefits. Helpers should challenge their own hidden commitments and help clients notice and challenge theirs.

Eula was busy with useful activities but produced no product; her counsellor helped her see that over-preparation and half-finished work reflected fear. This was Andreou's second-order procrastination - delaying the solution to procrastination itself. Once she finished one product, others followed.

Mara procrastinates only when she needs to be assertive, as with her alumni volunteering, which led to insight about her "selflessness."

Kotter says change needs urgency, but true urgency (right things, timely) differs from false urgency (frenzied activity going nowhere). Partnoy adds that procrastination can be good when delay allows thought about consequences.

Helpers therefore look beyond laziness: Eula was not lazy at all. They help clients identify the fears and hidden commitments behind delay, distinguish busy-ness from progress on the critical actions, and judge whether a given delay is prudent reflection or avoidance.

practice.q: Explain learned helplessness and vicious circles as forms of client inertia.
practice.answer:
Inertia is the tendency to put off problem-managing action. Two of its forms are:

Learned helplessness. Seligman's concept, linked with depression, describes clients who learn early that nothing can be done about certain situations; feelings range from mild "I'm not up to this" to total helplessness with deep depression. It is a step beyond passivity. Bennett and Bennett saw a positive side: if problems truly are beyond control, illusory control and excessive self-blame do not help, and challenging self-blame fostered realistic hope. Helpers teach clients what is and is not in their control, as with a man who cannot change his disability but controls how he views it. The opposite is learned optimism and resourcefulness; since optimism has costs (Chang), Egan suggests aiming for hopeful realists.

Vicious circles. Pyszczynski and Greenberg proposed that failure leads to lost self-worth, constant self-focus, negative affect and further failure, with a negative self-image that explains one's plight and maintains depression. Amanda, unaware of office politics, spiralled into mistakes and complaints. Her counsellor addressed the whole circle and her problem solving, so small successes created a benign circle.

Both forms show how inertia keeps clients from acting even when sound plans exist. Egan's general advice is that helpers add value by helping clients challenge disabling self-talk while also helping them act in their lives, because inner change and outer problem-solving success reinforce each other.

practice.q: Write a note on 'choosing not to change'.
practice.answer:
Egan observes that some clients do well at analysing problems, setting goals and identifying reasonable strategies, yet end up saying, in effect, that although they understand themselves and what they need to do, they do not want to pay the price action calls for; more effective living costs too much.

He finds human motivation as enigmatic now as ever: people often choose their own misery and stew in it rather than endure the relatively short-lived pain of behavioural change.

The helper's role: invite clients to challenge themselves to search for incentives and rewards for managing their lives better, and help them understand the consequences of not changing. But in the end it is the client's choice.

This contrasts with Vicky's determined action. Savvy helpers are not magicians but understand the shadow side of change, spot its signs in each case and, in line with the values of Chapter 2, invite clients to deal with the shadow side of themselves and their world. Box 14.2 ends with the guideline that helpers must face up to the fact that not every client wants to change.

Egan's position therefore balances two values: helpers should not be passive or give up on reluctant clients, yet they must respect client self-responsibility and accept that the final decision about paying the price of change belongs to the client.

practice.q: Describe the key ingredients of successful therapy as revisited by Egan at the end of The Skilled Helper.
practice.answer:
Egan urges helpers to become experts in the basics and spend their careers augmenting them, letting the basics permeate any chosen approach.

The Client: helping is first about the client; client needs should arbitrate disputes; befriending diversity is key.
The Therapist: live the basics, be genuine (helping is not theatre); clients, not therapists, have a success rate.
The Helping Relationship: make each interaction a learning event; collaboration is its heart.
Communication Skills: prize and develop them, use them everywhere, make dialogue the default.
Feedback: in every session, on between-session progress and session helpfulness, without denying clients self-challenge.
The Treatment Approach: important but not the most important; choose one you can communicate easily; helping is a journey taken together.
Problem Management: present in every approach; not an add-on.
Decision Making: master its dynamics and shadow side, as helpers make and coach decisions.
Beliefs-Values-Norms-Ethics-Morality: they drive behaviour and permeate helping; ethics is not an add-on.

Each ingredient brings uncertainties; therapy deals with them daily, so helpers must become professional jugglers.

His message is that the book is contemporary rather than the last word on therapy: whatever approach helpers choose, these basics should permeate both its structure and its delivery, and should be lived in the helper's own life, not just practised in sessions.

practice.q: Write a short note on posttraumatic growth.
practice.answer:
Posttraumatic growth is a growing area of literature (Calhoun & Tedeschi; Joseph; Joseph & Linley; Tedeschi & Calhoun). Egan describes it as related to outcome resilience but going beyond it: not just returning to a former state but growing.

Research: Phillips and Daniluk, exploring seven adult women abused as children, found a strong sense of resiliency and growth throughout their stories; one felt the experience taught her how unlimited the human spirit is. Bogar and Hulse-Killacky, studying ten such women, identified resiliency determinants (interpersonally skilled, competent, high self-regard, spiritual, helpful life circumstances) and resiliency processes (coping strategies, refocusing and moving on, active healing, achieving closure). Park, Lechner, Antoni and Stanton showed medical illness can lead to positive change.

Caution: such research is socially and culturally tricky. Stephen Joseph advises therapists to be aware of the potential for positive change but not to imply trauma is inherently positive; growth originates within the person through struggling with the event and its aftermath. Helpers can support clients in that struggle.

Egan concludes that some clients can somehow use the horror of abuse, torture or almost any disorder as a stimulus for growth, and that helpers can be glad this is possible and can help clients in their struggle to benefit from it.

practice.q: Define strategy, tactics and logistics.
practice.answer: A strategy is a practical plan or programme for accomplishing an objective. Tactics is the art of adapting the plan to the immediate situation, including changing it on the spot for unforeseen complications. Logistics is the art of providing needed resources in a timely way. Rebecca kept her course plan, adapted to a prepayment demand and found a cheaper college.

practice.q: What is second-order procrastination?
practice.answer: Andreou's term for procrastinating on implementing a solution to procrastination itself. Eula was very active - researching, attending seminars, drafting plans - but avoided the most critical actions of finishing and marketing products, out of fear of starting the business.

practice.q: Distinguish lapse from relapse.
practice.answer: Brownell and associates distinguished a lapse - a slip or mistake in an action programme - from a relapse - giving up the programme entirely. A lapse need not become a relapse. Helpers prepare clients for mistakes without giving "permission." Graham occasionally loses his temper but keeps going.

practice.q: What is extinction in the context of implementation?
practice.answer: Extinction is the process by which constructive-change activities that are not rewarded lose vigour, decrease and disappear. Luigi's soup-kitchen work became a "should" rather than a "want"; moving to more challenging work restored his energy. Incentives need tending.

practice.q: What is social facilitation?
practice.answer: Social facilitation is enlisting friends' help in a change effort. Wing and Jeffery found weight-loss clients who did so were much more successful than those going solo. It differs from dependence: facilitation energises, whereas dependence tends to limit and depress.

practice.q: Distinguish outcome resilience from process resilience.
practice.answer: Holaday and McPhearson's outcome resilience implies a return to a previous state - "bounce back," like Dora after divorce. Process resilience is the continuous effort to cope that is a normal part of some people's lives, like Nadia with chronic fatigue syndrome.

practice.q: Distinguish inertia from entropy.
practice.answer: Inertia is the human tendency to put off problem-managing action - never starting (e.g. passivity, learned helplessness, disorganisation). Entropy is the tendency to slow down and give up action that has already been initiated, which Kirschenbaum calls self-regulatory failure.

Most clients need to get on with their lives without a helper; avoid co-dependent relationships.
Channel highs; manage lows; don't disrupt others; no big decisions when high or low.
Price of action seen as too high; helpers invite, but it's the client's choice.
Client, therapist, relationship, communication skills, feedback, treatment approach, problem management, decision making, beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality.

summary: Stages I-III plan for change; the Action Arrow demands action that starts immediately, continues throughout and leads to preferred outcomes (p. 374).
Kirschenbaum lists many reasons clients fail to start or give up; Kanfer and Schefft distinguish decisional from protracted self-control (p. 375).
Mara, showing a bias toward action, reviews her goals: community, a more fulfilling career and an uncertain relationship goal with her parents (pp. 375-377).
Plans need strategy, tactics and logistics; most clients are not ready for action, so helpers bridge the gap patiently (pp. 377-378).
Procrastination stems from hidden commitments and immunity to change; watch for second-order procrastination and false urgency (pp. 378-379).
Imprudent action, like Elmer's, comes from unrealistic goals and grabbing the first strategy (pp. 379-380).
Force-field analysis identifies restraining and facilitating forces; 'forewarned is forearmed' (pp. 380-383).
Incentives must outweigh rewards for not acting; they need tending, backups and protection from extinction (pp. 383-385).
Self-contracts and commitment contracts (Karlan) focus energy; involving other stakeholders boosts progress (pp. 385-386).
Social support is a key resource; social facilitation helps, but social capital is declining and distress can drive supporters away (pp. 386-388).
Clients need challenging relationships, two-way feedback (confirmatory and corrective) and sensible use of checklists (pp. 388-391).

Shadow side: passive helpers, client inertia (passivity, learned helplessness, self-talk, vicious circles, disorganisation) and entropy (false hopes, discretionary change, decay curve, lapse vs relapse) (pp. 391-396).
Resilience - outcome and process - can be tapped even in desperate clients; factors include social support, cognitive skills and psychological resources (pp. 396-400).
Posttraumatic growth goes beyond outcome resilience but arises from the person's struggle, not the trauma (p. 400).
Most clients must eventually manage without a helper; co-dependent helping is a shadow side; Vicky shows what determined self-management can achieve (pp. 401-402).
Some clients choose not to change; helpers invite but the choice is theirs. Box 14.2 summarises action guidelines (pp. 402-403).
Egan closes by urging mastery of the basics of therapy and comfort with uncertainty (pp. 403-404).

assessment.q: Tom Morris's first two conditions for success correspond to which stages of the helping model?
assessment.explain: Egan says the first two refer to Stages II and III; the other five refer to implementation.

assessment.q: A client deciding to give up alcohol completely is exercising:
assessment.explain: A single choice terminating a conflict is decisional; handling later temptations is protracted.

assessment.q: Rebecca taking the course at a community college illustrates which combination?
options: Keeping the strategy, adapting with tactics and finding a resource (logistics)
assessment.explain: She kept her plan, adapted it and located another resource.

assessment.q: Kegan and Lahey's term for the personal set of factors that keeps people from changing is:
assessment.explain: Kegan and Lahey call this personal immunity to change.

assessment.q: Partnoy's view of procrastination is that:
options: There is good procrastination and bad
Procrastination is caused only by fear
assessment.explain: Delay can give time to consider consequences of acting too quickly.

assessment.q: In force-field analysis, Nora's Bible reading before dialysis is an example of a:
assessment.explain: The counsellor helped her substitute positive thinking, an underused resource.

assessment.q: Miguel's counsellor tried to replace fear with incentives arising from:
assessment.explain: The counsellor believed real incentives came from the decent person hidden under the tough exterior.

assessment.q: The NAMHC Task Force (1996) found social-support factors helped clinically depressed patients in about what proportion of studies?
assessment.explain: In about 75% of studies support increased initial success and maintenance of gains.

assessment.q: Putnam's term for informal connectedness and formal civic engagement is:
assessment.explain: Putnam showed social capital has fallen in North America.

assessment.q: Casey's recovery improved when his counsellor challenged him to:
options: Move closer to his family abroad
Ask for help from local friends
assessment.explain: He had hidden his illness to avoid being a burden; his friends and a church group helped.

assessment.q: Two-way feedback in Egan's sense means feedback on:
options: Progress toward outcomes at the start and on the session's value at the end
The client's personality and the therapist's personality
assessment.explain: Egan describes feedback at beginning and end of each session.

assessment.q: Passivity, according to Egan citing Schiff, can take the form of:
options: Doing nothing, uncritical acceptance, aimlessness, or paralysis/blowing up
assessment.explain: These forms are listed in the passivity subsection.

assessment.q: Egan suggests we help clients become:
assessment.explain: Optimism and pessimism each have costs; hopeful realism is suggested.

assessment.q: Driscoll's view of disorganisation and inertia is that they are:
options: A form of control clients can be helped to redirect
assessment.explain: Clients have been in the driver's seat all along; recognising this lets them redirect their power.

assessment.q: Egan's 'Okavango-Kalahari phenomenon' describes:
options: Change programmes that start vigorously but disappear
assessment.explain: Like floodwaters vanishing into the desert, discretionary change programmes disappear.

assessment.q: Phillips's 'ubiquitous decay curve' refers to:
options: Attrition, noncompliance and relapse in helping and medical care
The fading of fear after probation
assessment.explain: Phillips identified this curve in helping and medical-delivery situations.

assessment.q: Graham occasionally loses his temper but continues his programme. This shows:
options: A lapse that does not become a relapse
assessment.explain: Brownell distinguished a lapse (slip) from relapse (giving up entirely).

assessment.q: Which of the following is one of Bogar and Hulse-Killacky's 'resiliency processes'?
assessment.explain: Processes: coping strategies, refocusing and moving on, active healing, achieving closure; the others are determinants.

assessment.q: Egan describes the helping relationship becoming 'the problem rather than the solution' when:
options: Helper and client covertly conspire to maintain the relationship
The client joins a self-help group
The client sees the helper occasionally as needed
The helper prepares the client for ending
assessment.explain: This co-dependent relationship replaces life-enhancing outcomes with talk.

assessment.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the goals Vicky spelled out?
options: Channelling the energy of her highs
Being completely cured of bipolar disorder
Not making important decisions when high or low
assessment.explain: Egan says her goal was not to be cured but to lead as normal a life as possible.
